  - `D1-C501` **[Stage]** A community demo's script used both input modes of Google's Rich Results Test: the URL mode for public pages, which Google fetches itself, and the code mode, into which the script pasted the page's HTML, for private pages and pages Google cannot fetch (best reading of a largely unintelligible recording; the second kind of page was heard as 'dead', possibly 'dev').
  - `D1-C249` **[Stage]** A community demo showed a script that opens Chrome with a saved session, pastes a URL into Google's Rich Results Test, waits about 15 seconds, then screenshots and saves the result and retries on failure (the demo's recording is largely unintelligible; the tool name is a best reading).
- [`D1-C502`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI) extends [`D1-C251`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI)
  - `D1-C502` **[Stage]** In a community demo, the structured-data problems Google's Rich Results Test reported on the test page included an empty name, a breadcrumb problem and a price of zero, with errors shown in pink and warnings in orange (best readings of a largely unintelligible recording; each item is heard in only one of the two recordings).
  - `D1-C251` **[Stage]** A community demo treated warnings in Google's structured-data test as not critical, in an example result of 22 items with two errors and two warnings.
- [`D1-C503`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI) extends [`D1-C252`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI)
  - `D1-C503` **[Stage]** In a community demo, the small model choosing keywords (Claude Haiku) followed fixed rules, no brand terms, no navigation terms and at most two keywords per page; the Spanish example was 'zapatos de mujer' and 'comprar zapatos de mujer' (women's shoes, buy women's shoes).
  - `D1-C252` **[Stage]** A community demo matched model size to the task: a small, cheap model (Claude Haiku) chose keywords from a page's URL, title, H1, description and schema types, while a large, expensive model (Claude Opus) fixed code and wrote the summary.
- [`D1-C504`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (annotates Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI) extends [`D1-C294`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI)
  - `D1-C504` **[Analysis]** The study cited on stage matches Peec AI's analysis (reported in February 2026) of over 10 million ChatGPT prompts and 20 million fan-outs: 43% of the fan-out searches for non-English prompts ran in English, and nearly 78% of non-English prompt runs had at least one English fan-out (from 66% for Spanish to 94% for Turkish), so the 43% is a share of fan-out searches, not of prompts.
  - `D1-C294` **[Stage]** A community speaker cited a third-party study (heard as Peec AI's) finding that 43% of prompts produced fan-out queries in a language other than the one the user searched in.
- [`D1-C505`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (annotates Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI) extends [`D1-C271`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI)
  - `D1-C505` **[Analysis]** The llms.txt study cited on stage matches Ahrefs' June 2026 study of 137,210 domains: 28% (about 38,000, the 'almost 40,000' sites heard on stage) published an llms.txt file and 97% of those files received no requests at all in May 2026; the files that were fetched got about 22,000 requests across some 1,100 domains, around 20 each, not the 'two hits a month' heard on stage.
  - `D1-C271` **[Stage]** A community speaker said llms.txt files are not necessary, citing a third-party study from summer 2026 (heard as Ahrefs') that looked at almost 40,000 sites over one month: 97% had no AI agent hits on the file, and those that had any got about two hits a month.
- [`D1-C506`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (annotates Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI) extends [`D1-C249`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI)
  - `D1-C506` **[Docs]** Google's Rich Results Test help says the tool tests either a page's full URL or a pasted code snippet (Code instead of URL); all page resources must be reachable by an anonymous user on the internet, so resources behind a firewall or a password are not available to the test unless exposed, for example through a tunnel.
  - `D1-C249` **[Stage]** A community demo showed a script that opens Chrome with a saved session, pastes a URL into Google's Rich Results Test, waits about 15 seconds, then screenshots and saves the result and retries on failure (the demo's recording is largely unintelligible; the tool name is a best reading).
- [`D1-C066`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) extends [`D1-C326`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D1-C066` **[Slide]** Google Search, Ads, Shopping and Images all request through one centralised crawling infrastructure, whose primary mandate is to fetch from the internet while strictly preventing the overloading of external servers.
  - `D1-C326` **[Stage]** Google does not let each team build its own crawler: its many crawlers share one crawler infrastructure, because every crawler must accomplish a few specific tasks and obey Google's internal crawling policies.
- [`D1-C325`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works) extends [`D1-C038`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D1-C325` **[Stage]** Googlebot is the crawler Google uses for web search, including Search's AI features.
  - `D1-C038` **[Slide]** AI Mode and AI Overviews use the same crawling and the same index as Search. At serving they add grounding on the Search index and query fan-out.
- [`D1-C335`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works) extends [`D1-C039`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D1-C335` **[Stage]** Crawling for Gemini may be set to care less about quality and more about the amount of content, because for large language models the number of tokens matters more than quality.
  - `D1-C039` **[Slide]** Gemini is not part of Search, but it uses crawlers for data, shares some technologies such as tokenization and deduping, and grounds on the Search index.
- [`D1-C336`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works) extends [`D1-C040`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D1-C336` **[Stage]** Google finds what to crawl mainly by extracting URLs from previously crawled pages, and additionally from sitemaps.
  - `D1-C040` **[Slide]** URL discovery works through links: a homepage links to section pages, which link to further pages.
- [`D1-C359`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search) extends [`D1-C069`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D1-C359` **[Stage]** Most network errors happen somewhere between the site's origin server and Google's data centers, where they are invisible to both Google and the site owner; the way TCP networks work leaves no way to see what went wrong there.
  - `D1-C069` **[Stage]** DNS issues and firewalls are blind spots: Google does not know a firewall is blocking it, it only sees that requests fail.
- [`D1-C508`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search) extends [`D1-C368`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D1-C508` **[Stage]** Google said soft 404s, like some other problem categories, are looked up in Search Console's page indexing report, while other crawl issues are debugged in the Crawl Stats report.
  - `D1-C368` **[Stage]** Search Console's page indexing report breaks down the reasons why pages do or do not show in Search, and its categories help find patterns in how a site's content is crawled and served to Google's crawlers.
- [`D1-C508`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search) extends [`D1-C367`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D1-C508` **[Stage]** Google said soft 404s, like some other problem categories, are looked up in Search Console's page indexing report, while other crawl issues are debugged in the Crawl Stats report.
  - `D1-C367` **[Stage]** CDN captcha challenges often return HTTP 200; Googlebot does not solve them and sees only content with a 200 status, which indexing then classifies as a soft 404, reported as an error in Search Console.
- [`D1-C509`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search) extends [`D1-C366`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D1-C509` **[Stage]** Google has seen an uptick in 402 Payment Required responses to its crawlers, an even more recent trend than the rise in 403 responses.
  - `D1-C366` **[Stage]** Google treats a 402 Payment Required response as a 404 Not Found, because Googlebot cannot pay for content.
- [`D1-C509`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search) extends [`D1-C365`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D1-C509` **[Stage]** Google has seen an uptick in 402 Payment Required responses to its crawlers, an even more recent trend than the rise in 403 responses.
  - `D1-C365` **[Stage]** Google has recently seen more 403 responses to its crawlers (described on stage as 'authentication required'); it treats them as client errors, technically equivalent to 404 or 410, and drops those pages from Search and its AI features.
- [`D1-C512`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C329`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D1-C512` **[Stage]** Robots.txt is now an IETF standard, RFC 9309, supported by basically all major crawlers; Google said it follows it because it is the right thing to do: anyone who wants to opt out of crawling should be able to.
  - `D1-C329` **[Stage]** Apart from contractual crawlers, all of Google's automated crawlers obey robots.txt, which Google treats as the way site owners opt out of its crawling.
- [`D1-C513`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C086`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C513` **[Stage]** The standard's official name is the Robots Exclusion Protocol (REP). Google stressed that it was designed in 1994 only to control which automated clients may access what on a site, and has nothing to do with how the content is used.
  - `D1-C086` **[Docs]** Google-Extended is a control token, not a crawler with its own user agent string. It decides whether crawled content may be used to train future Gemini models and to ground Gemini apps and Vertex AI.
- [`D1-C516`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C084`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C516` **[Stage]** Robots.txt was made extremely simple by design so that anyone could implement and understand it; it was extended as websites grew more complex, but it still has only three rules: user-agent (a named crawler, or * for every crawler), disallow and allow.
  - `D1-C084` **[Docs]** Google supports only the user-agent, allow, disallow and sitemap fields in robots.txt. Other fields such as crawl-delay are not supported.
- [`D1-C519`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C080`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C519` **[Stage]** A user-agent line with its allow and disallow rules forms a user-agent group, and one group can name several crawlers (the talk's example: Googlebot and Bingbot); give named crawlers their own group only when they need rules the * group should not grant to every crawler.
  - `D1-C080` **[Docs]** Rules can be grouped for several crawlers by repeating user-agent lines. A crawler follows only the most specific group that names it.
- [`D1-C520`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C079`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C520` **[Stage]** In the talk's worked example, disallow /*/live/ blocks /science/live/ and /sports/live/, because * matches any number of characters, and an allow /science/live/ rule re-opens that one path.
  - `D1-C079` **[Slide]** The robots.txt session worked through an example file with three groups: a default group that disallows everything except the bare homepage, a shared bingbot and googlebot group that also allows /politics/ and /*/live/, and a google-extended group that disallows /subscriptions/.
- [`D1-C520`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C081`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C520` **[Stage]** In the talk's worked example, disallow /*/live/ blocks /science/live/ and /sports/live/, because * matches any number of characters, and an allow /science/live/ rule re-opens that one path.
  - `D1-C081` **[Docs]** When matching rules to a URL, Google uses the most specific rule by path length. If rules conflict, it uses the least restrictive one.
- [`D1-C521`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C079`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C521` **[Stage]** To let unnamed crawlers fetch only the homepage, use user-agent: *, disallow: / and allow: /$; the $ ends the match, so /$ means only the root path and /cats$ means exactly /cats.
  - `D1-C079` **[Slide]** The robots.txt session worked through an example file with three groups: a default group that disallows everything except the bare homepage, a shared bingbot and googlebot group that also allows /politics/ and /*/live/, and a google-extended group that disallows /subscriptions/.
- [`D1-C521`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C082`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C521` **[Stage]** To let unnamed crawlers fetch only the homepage, use user-agent: *, disallow: / and allow: /$; the $ ends the match, so /$ means only the root path and /cats$ means exactly /cats.
  - `D1-C082` **[Docs]** In robots.txt, * matches zero or more of any character and $ marks the end of the URL.
- [`D1-C522`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C086`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C522` **[Stage]** Google said a site can keep a directory or the whole site out of Gemini model training by disallowing it for the Google-Extended token in robots.txt, and that Google respects that policy; the speaker believed Google was the first to offer such an opt-out from model training.
  - `D1-C086` **[Docs]** Google-Extended is a control token, not a crawler with its own user agent string. It decides whether crawled content may be used to train future Gemini models and to ground Gemini apps and Vertex AI.
- [`D1-C523`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C086`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C523` **[Analysis]** The 'first' needs care: OpenAI documented how to block its GPTBot crawler in robots.txt in August 2023, before Google announced Google-Extended on 28 September 2023. What Google-Extended added was a token that controls AI-training use of pages fetched by Google's existing crawlers, separately from Search; Apple later introduced a similar token, Applebot-Extended.
  - `D1-C086` **[Docs]** Google-Extended is a control token, not a crawler with its own user agent string. It decides whether crawled content may be used to train future Gemini models and to ground Gemini apps and Vertex AI.
- [`D1-C526`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C087`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C526` **[Stage]** The real trouble is an unknown line placed between two user-agent lines: while writing RFC 9309, Google asked people whether the first crawler should then inherit the rules that follow, and opinions split roughly 50-50 (how the talk said the question was settled is unclear in the recording).
  - `D1-C087` **[Slide]** Googlebot ignores an unknown line, such as a Content-signal line, placed between two user-agent lines and joins both user agents into one group, so the rules that follow apply to both; in the slide's example both are blocked.
- [`D1-C526`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C123`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C526` **[Stage]** The real trouble is an unknown line placed between two user-agent lines: while writing RFC 9309, Google asked people whether the first crawler should then inherit the rules that follow, and opinions split roughly 50-50 (how the talk said the question was settled is unclear in the recording).
  - `D1-C123` **[Slide]** Bing closes the robots.txt group at an unknown line placed between two user-agent lines, so in the slide's example bingbot ends up not blocked while Googlebot is; the slide warned that different crawlers behave differently.
- [`D1-C527`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C080`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C527` **[Stage]** The talk's fix for giving one crawler both an extra rule and the rules of another group: simply add another group for that crawler. Google's spec combines all groups that name the same user agent into one.
  - `D1-C080` **[Docs]** Rules can be grouped for several crawlers by repeating user-agent lines. A crawler follows only the most specific group that names it.
- [`D1-C528`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C140`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C528` **[Stage]** Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt file as Google last fetched it, with a version history and the errors and successes of each fetch.
  - `D1-C140` **[Docs]** Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt files Google found for the top 20 hosts of a Domain property, with their fetch status, warnings and errors; to test whether a specific URL is blocked, Google's help page points to the URL Inspection tool and to Google's open-source robots.txt library.
- [`D1-C530`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C140`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C530` **[Stage]** Google said the robots.txt report uses the parser Google open-sourced at github.com/google/robotstxt.
  - `D1-C140` **[Docs]** Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt files Google found for the top 20 hosts of a Domain property, with their fetch status, warnings and errors; to test whether a specific URL is blocked, Google's help page points to the URL Inspection tool and to Google's open-source robots.txt library.
- [`D1-C531`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C080`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C531` **[Stage]** In the talk's quiz, the answer for letting Googlebot crawl /staging/preview/ while keeping the rest of /staging/ closed to it was a user-agent: googlebot group with both rules, disallow /staging/ and allow /staging/preview/, rather than an allow in the * group or a Googlebot group with only the allow.
  - `D1-C080` **[Docs]** Rules can be grouped for several crawlers by repeating user-agent lines. A crawler follows only the most specific group that names it.
- [`D1-C532`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt) extends [`D1-C525`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C532` **[Analysis]** A typo in a rule name is not always ignored by Google: its open-source robots.txt parser deliberately accepts common misspellings of disallow (such as dissallow, dissalow and disalow) and of user-agent (useragent, user agent), but not of allow. Google's spec page does not mention typos, and other crawlers may be stricter, so spell rule names correctly.
  - `D1-C525` **[Stage]** Google called robots.txt extremely forgiving: a typo in a path only blocks the wrong path, a typo in a rule name such as disallow makes Google ignore that line, and the rest of the file is still used.
- [`D1-C533`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, Lightning session B: Robots.txt) extends [`D1-C080`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D1-C533` **[Stage]** Dave Smart said robots.txt groups are not additive: if a group matches a crawler's user agent, only that group's rules apply, so a googlebot group that blocks /dogs/ leaves Googlebot free to crawl the /goats/ and /cows/ that the * group blocks.
  - `D1-C080` **[Docs]** Rules can be grouped for several crawlers by repeating user-agent lines. A crawler follows only the most specific group that names it.
- [`D1-C373`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) extends [`D1-C096`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C373` **[Stage]** Crawl budget is the finite amount of resources Google allocates to crawling a specific website, and it determines how many of the site's pages are discovered and how often they are revisited.
  - `D1-C096` **[Stage]** Crawl budget was described as the attention span Google gives a website, and better performance increases it.
- [`D1-C374`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) extends [`D1-C091`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C374` **[Stage]** Crawl rate limit, or hostload, is a proxy for how many requests per second the connection to a site can handle before Google hits the limit.
  - `D1-C091` **[Slide]** Crawl rate limit, or hostload, is a host-wide metric shared across all Google crawlers.
- [`D1-C375`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) extends [`D1-C066`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C375` **[Stage]** Googlebot as a single standalone crawler is a historical idea: Google crawls through a centralised crawling infrastructure, so a request from a Google user agent in server logs is a request routed through that shared platform.
  - `D1-C066` **[Slide]** Google Search, Ads, Shopping and Images all request through one centralised crawling infrastructure, whose primary mandate is to fetch from the internet while strictly preventing the overloading of external servers.
- [`D1-C376`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) extends [`D1-C091`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C376` **[Stage]** Hostload applies per host, not necessarily per site: depending on how a site is configured, its CDN, its app, its subdomains and its main www host may be different hosts.
  - `D1-C091` **[Slide]** Crawl rate limit, or hostload, is a host-wide metric shared across all Google crawlers.
- [`D1-C377`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) extends [`D1-C093`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C377` **[Stage]** The quality that drives crawl demand is the quality of the site as a whole, not the quality of an individual page.
  - `D1-C093` **[Slide]** Crawl demand is driven by the quality of the site, the change frequency of its URLs and their popularity on the internet.
- [`D1-C378`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) extends [`D1-C099`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C378` **[Stage]** Google treats URLs that differ as different URLs and crawls all of them even when they lead to the same content, so infinite URL spaces such as calendars or many versions of a page burn crawl budget.
  - `D1-C099` **[Slide]** Three things burn crawl budget: server errors unrelated to server load, useless pages and resources, and infinite URL spaces.
- [`D1-C379`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) extends [`D1-C103`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C379` **[Stage]** The useless content worth improving or removing to save crawl budget includes very bad or low-quality pages, spam content, duplicate pages and soft error pages.
  - `D1-C103` **[Slide]** Four ways to manage crawl budget: use HTTP cache control, have good site navigation, restrict crawlers' access to faceted navigation and action URLs, and improve or remove useless content.
- [`D1-C388`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) extends [`D1-C038`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D1-C388` **[Stage]** AI Mode is a feature that sits on top of Google's existing crawling infrastructure, so Google does not crawl a site more because of AI Mode.
  - `D1-C038` **[Slide]** AI Mode and AI Overviews use the same crawling and the same index as Search. At serving they add grounding on the Search index and query fan-out.
- [`D1-C404`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S11-lightning-session-c-crawling.md) (Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling) extends [`D1-C102`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C404` **[Stage]** For query parameters, a community speaker advised checking that every parameter in a request is actually used and in the expected order, and otherwise redirecting to the expected URL with only the used parameters in the correct order.
  - `D1-C102` **[Docs]** If faceted URLs must be crawled, use the standard & separator, keep filters in a consistent order, and return a 404 when a filter combination has no results.
- [`D1-C412`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S11-lightning-session-c-crawling.md) (Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling) extends [`D1-C053`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (annotates Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D1-C412` **[Stage]** A community speaker described AI search as turning one query into many related searches, including searches in other languages, before the information is retrieved.
  - `D1-C053` **[Docs]** Query fan-out means running several related searches at once to gather more results; a question about lawn weeds may also search herbicides and weed prevention.
- [`D1-C433`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (annotates Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C432`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C433` **[Analysis]** The crawler best practices mentioned on stage match the public IETF Internet-Draft 'Crawler best practices' (draft-illyes-aipref-cbcp-00, July 2025), which says self-declared research crawlers, including privacy and malware discovery crawlers, may exempt themselves from any of its practices with a rationale; it is a draft, not Google documentation.
  - `D1-C432` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said they were working on a set of crawler best practices and offering research, malware-scanning and privacy crawlers an exemption from following them, apparently because such crawlers sometimes need to ignore robots.txt or probe URLs that other crawlers would not touch (the reason is a best reading: the audio has 'don't need', which would not explain an exemption).
- [`D1-C439`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C093`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C439` **[Stage]** Very large, constantly changing sites get no special handling: when URLs change frequently or are useful to users, Google raises crawl demand and tries to raise its crawl capacity for the site, the same logic it applies to small sites.
  - `D1-C093` **[Slide]** Crawl demand is driven by the quality of the site, the change frequency of its URLs and their popularity on the internet.
- [`D1-C444`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C397`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S11-lightning-session-c-crawling.md) (Day 1, Lightning session C: Crawling)
  - `D1-C444` **[Stage]** Log files are worth checking on sites with filter parameters or complicated URLs, because crawlers can easily wander off into URLs that make no sense for the site.
  - `D1-C397` **[Stage]** A community speaker said similar URLs are an indicator of duplicate content, broken links, unnecessary redirects and other technical issues.
- [`D1-C470`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (annotates Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C469`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C470` **[Analysis]** Google's crawl budget guide says crawl budget freed by robots.txt blocks is not shifted to other pages unless the site already hits its crawl capacity limit, and advises against robots.txt for temporary reallocation; so block only sections you never want crawled, and expect a shift only on capacity-limited sites.
  - `D1-C469` **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said disallowing a section that should not be crawled, such as /ads, in a Googlebot group in robots.txt shifts crawl budget to the rest of the site.
- [`D1-C480`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (annotates Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C477`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C480` **[Analysis]** The consolidation described on stage matches Google's November 2020 move from Google Webmasters to Google Search Central, which moved its main blog, 13 localized blogs and the Search help content of the Search Console Help Center to its developer site: about six years before the event, not the four or five said on stage.
  - `D1-C477` **[Stage]** In a migration about four or five years before the event, Google consolidated 12 or 14 of its blogs in different languages, a Help Center and its old developers site into one site.
- [`D1-C538`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C439`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C538` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said crawl demand is not only Search's: when enough of a site's URLs are wanted by Search, Google Ads or another Google product, Google raises the site's crawl demand and crawls up to that level of demand as far as the site's crawl capacity allows.
  - `D1-C439` **[Stage]** Very large, constantly changing sites get no special handling: when URLs change frequently or are useful to users, Google raises crawl demand and tries to raise its crawl capacity for the site, the same logic it applies to small sites.
- [`D1-C538`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C334`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D1-C538` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said crawl demand is not only Search's: when enough of a site's URLs are wanted by Search, Google Ads or another Google product, Google raises the site's crawl demand and crawls up to that level of demand as far as the site's crawl capacity allows.
  - `D1-C334` **[Stage]** Different Google teams prioritise crawling differently: web search cares a lot about the quality of a site and its content, while Ads wants to check every publisher page that wants to appear in Google Ads, so it schedules those URLs as they come in.
- [`D1-C539`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C447`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C539` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said useless plugin-generated parameter URLs can be handled at the web server, for example with a rule or a custom module in Apache, which saves crawl budget so that Google may pick up the URLs that matter instead (the exact mechanism is not clear in the recording).
  - `D1-C447` **[Stage]** Google crawls new URLs, such as plugin-generated calendar pages, because it wants to see what they are; its automated systems learn that such URLs are useless only from large samples, which takes time.
- [`D1-C539`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C446`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C539` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said useless plugin-generated parameter URLs can be handled at the web server, for example with a rule or a custom module in Apache, which saves crawl budget so that Google may pick up the URLs that matter instead (the exact mechanism is not clear in the recording).
  - `D1-C446` **[Stage]** Many crawling complaints that reach Google's crawling team turn out to be caused by a plugin, for example a WordPress calendar plugin that adds calendar parameters to the URLs of every post, page, category and tag page.
- [`D1-C541`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C479`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C541` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said, as a fun fact, that JavaScript was used for the language-consolidation redirects in Google's own site migration, because it was the only option available to the person doing it (the recording does not make fully clear whether the JavaScript performed the redirects or built the mapping).
  - `D1-C479` **[Stage]** Where content was duplicated across languages, Google's own site consolidation redirected two language versions into one, giving both old URLs one target path to redirect to.
- [`D1-C542`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (annotates Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C541`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C542` **[Analysis]** Google's redirects guide says Google Search follows JavaScript location redirects only after rendering, may never see one if rendering fails, and should be used only when server-side or meta refresh redirects are impossible; its site move guide asks for server-side permanent redirects (301 or 308) where technically possible. The JavaScript in Google's own migration was a fallback ('my only option'), not a pattern to copy.
  - `D1-C541` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said, as a fun fact, that JavaScript was used for the language-consolidation redirects in Google's own site migration, because it was the only option available to the person doing it (the recording does not make fully clear whether the JavaScript performed the redirects or built the mapping).
- [`D1-C543`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C467`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C543` **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said that if the time from publishing to Googlebot's first crawl starts rising, how much it rises matters: for the crawling of fresh stories, something like two hours is probably not great (a smaller example figure is unclear in the recording).
  - `D1-C467` **[Stage]** To check that new content is crawled fast enough, Gary Illyes advised measuring the time between publishing a URL and Googlebot's first crawl of it: ideally it stays flat or falls, and only a rising trend calls for investigation.
- [`D1-C544`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C492`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C544` **[Stage]** John Mueller said that if the Crawl Stats report shows about half of a site's crawling going to discovering new pages, that is a lot of discovery crawling, which suggests that crawling of new pages is not the problem.
  - `D1-C492` **[Stage]** John Mueller said the Crawl Stats report's split of crawling by purpose, discovery versus refresh, gives a rough view of whether discovery crawling is in a reasonable range, though measuring publish-to-first-crawl time is more accurate.
- [`D1-C546`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C374`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C546` **[Stage]** A Google panelist illustrated a crawl capacity limit drop as a step down in the site's hostload, for example from 10 to 5, which the panelist said means Googlebot then makes up to five requests per second (the recording adds 'per connection', which is unclear).
  - `D1-C374` **[Stage]** Crawl rate limit, or hostload, is a proxy for how many requests per second the connection to a site can handle before Google hits the limit.
- [`D1-C547`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (annotates Day 1, Q&A) extends [`D1-C546`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C547` **[Analysis]** Google's crawl budget guide does not express the crawl capacity limit in requests per second: it limits the total time a server spends holding connections open for Google, counting both the number of parallel connections and their duration. That fits the panel's advice to watch how many connections Googlebot opens (D1-C494): fewer connections is the documented form of a lower capacity limit.
  - `D1-C546` **[Stage]** A Google panelist illustrated a crawl capacity limit drop as a step down in the site's hostload, for example from 10 to 5, which the panelist said means Googlebot then makes up to five requests per second (the recording adds 'per connection', which is unclear).
- [`D2-C820`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D1-C040`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C820` **[Slide]** Google's Q&A slide advised large sites to rely on hub pages, such as category pages, that link out to their important pages, instead of on HTML sitemaps.
  - `D1-C040` **[Slide]** URL discovery works through links: a homepage links to section pages, which link to further pages.
- [`D2-C820`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D1-C202`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C820` **[Slide]** Google's Q&A slide advised large sites to rely on hub pages, such as category pages, that link out to their important pages, instead of on HTML sitemaps.
  - `D1-C202` **[Stage]** Google may visit hub pages, such as a homepage or category pages, more often than other pages, because they usually link out to new or updated pages.
- [`D2-C017`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D1-C084`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D2-C017` **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that a sitemap listed in the robots.txt file can be picked up by any crawler, not only by Google's.
  - `D1-C084` **[Docs]** Google supports only the user-agent, allow, disallow and sitemap fields in robots.txt. Other fields such as crawl-delay are not supported.
- [`D2-C017`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D1-C079`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D2-C017` **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that a sitemap listed in the robots.txt file can be picked up by any crawler, not only by Google's.
  - `D1-C079` **[Slide]** The robots.txt session worked through an example file with three groups: a default group that disallows everything except the bare homepage, a shared bingbot and googlebot group that also allows /politics/ and /*/live/, and a google-extended group that disallows /subscriptions/.
- [`D2-C020`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D1-C110`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C020` **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as a noindex because some extremely important sites disallow their most important pages, by accident or out of ignorance.
  - `D1-C110` **[Analysis]** A URL blocked in robots.txt can still be indexed without its content if other pages link to it, and Google cannot see a noindex on a page it is not allowed to fetch.
- [`D2-C021`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D1-C105`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C021` **[Slide]** Google's Q&A slide said Google does not index the content of pages disallowed in robots.txt, but users will still find the URLs of those pages in Search.
  - `D1-C105` **[Slide]** URLs disallowed through robots.txt do not affect crawl budget, because they are not fetched.
- [`D2-C022`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D1-C106`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C022` **[Docs]** Google's noindex documentation says the noindex rule works only if the page is not blocked by robots.txt: a crawler that cannot fetch the page never sees the rule, and the page can still appear in search results, for example if other pages link to it.
  - `D1-C106` **[Slide]** The noindex rule consumes crawl budget, because Google must fetch the page to see it.
- [`D2-C838`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D2-C820`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C838` **[Stage]** Answering whether HTML sitemaps still matter for large sites, Google said a site that wants one can make one, but that the effort is better spent on hub pages such as category pages.
  - `D2-C820` **[Slide]** Google's Q&A slide advised large sites to rely on hub pages, such as category pages, that link out to their important pages, instead of on HTML sitemaps.
- [`D2-C841`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D2-C010`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C841` **[Stage]** Google contrasted out-of-stock products a buyer will wait for, such as a rare watch battery that matters to them, with easily replaced products, such as a particular cheese, for which the buyer simply picks a similar product instead of waiting.
  - `D2-C010` **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that whether to keep a temporarily out-of-stock product page or redirect it depends on how important that product page is to users.

  - `D2-C842` **[Stage]** Google said listing the sitemap in robots.txt is fine, as many websites do.
  - `D1-C084` **[Docs]** Google supports only the user-agent, allow, disallow and sitemap fields in robots.txt. Other fields such as crawl-delay are not supported.
- [`D2-C843`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D2-C017`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C843` **[Stage]** Google pointed out the trade-off of listing a sitemap in robots.txt: anyone can then see the sitemap, which a site may not want.

- [`D2-C844`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D2-C020`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C844` **[Stage]** Google illustrated why it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as noindex with an extremely important site, such as a national tax authority, that blocks very important PDF files with robots.txt: Google cannot index the PDFs' content but can at least show their URLs in search results.
  - `D2-C020` **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as a noindex because some extremely important sites disallow their most important pages, by accident or out of ignorance.
- [`D2-C846`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D2-C021`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C846` **[Stage]** Google said a URL disallowed by robots.txt might still be indexed if the URL is important, in which case the URL is indexed but not its content.
  - `D2-C021` **[Slide]** Google's Q&A slide said Google does not index the content of pages disallowed in robots.txt, but users will still find the URLs of those pages in Search.
- [`D2-C846`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D1-C110`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C846` **[Stage]** Google said a URL disallowed by robots.txt might still be indexed if the URL is important, in which case the URL is indexed but not its content.
  - `D1-C110` **[Analysis]** A URL blocked in robots.txt can still be indexed without its content if other pages link to it, and Google cannot see a noindex on a page it is not allowed to fetch.
- [`D2-C849`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) extends [`D1-C110`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C849` **[Analysis]** Google's robots.txt introduction names links from elsewhere on the web as the reason a disallowed URL can still be indexed, while on stage Google spoke of the URL's importance; either way, well-linked important URLs are the disallowed ones most likely to appear in results, so keep such pages crawlable with noindex if they must stay out of Search.
  - `D1-C110` **[Analysis]** A URL blocked in robots.txt can still be indexed without its content if other pages link to it, and Google cannot see a noindex on a page it is not allowed to fetch.
- [`D2-C024`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted) extends [`D1-C063`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D2-C024` **[Slide]** A Google slide titled Data from Crawling showed an example of what the crawler passes on for processing: the fetch result, the connect time and the time to first byte in milliseconds, the robots policies that apply to the fetch, and the raw HTTP response with the page's HTML.
  - `D1-C063` **[Slide]** The crawl pipeline runs from a crawl queue to a scheduler to the crawler, which fetches from the internet and passes the fetch reply to indexing.
- [`D2-C024`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted) extends [`D1-C064`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D2-C024` **[Slide]** A Google slide titled Data from Crawling showed an example of what the crawler passes on for processing: the fetch result, the connect time and the time to first byte in milliseconds, the robots policies that apply to the fetch, and the raw HTTP response with the page's HTML.
  - `D1-C064` **[Slide]** The crawler has multiple tasks: fetch from the internet, ensure it doesn't break the internet, and enforce robots.txt policies. Fetched data is sent for indexing.
- [`D2-C024`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted) extends [`D1-C092`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C024` **[Slide]** A Google slide titled Data from Crawling showed an example of what the crawler passes on for processing: the fetch result, the connect time and the time to first byte in milliseconds, the robots policies that apply to the fetch, and the raw HTTP response with the page's HTML.
  - `D1-C092` **[Slide]** Hostload is driven by changes in connect time, changes in time to first byte, and HTTP 429 or 5xx status codes. If these increase, hostload is adjusted and crawling slows down.
- [`D2-C025`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted) extends [`D1-C086`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D2-C025` **[Slide]** In Google's example fetch record, the robots policies that apply to a fetch, shown as the value opt-out-google-extended, travel with the fetched page into processing.
  - `D1-C086` **[Docs]** Google-Extended is a control token, not a crawler with its own user agent string. It decides whether crawled content may be used to train future Gemini models and to ground Gemini apps and Vertex AI.
- [`D2-C025`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted) extends [`D1-C064`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D2-C025` **[Slide]** In Google's example fetch record, the robots policies that apply to a fetch, shown as the value opt-out-google-extended, travel with the fetched page into processing.
  - `D1-C064` **[Slide]** The crawler has multiple tasks: fetch from the internet, ensure it doesn't break the internet, and enforce robots.txt policies. Fetched data is sent for indexing.
- [`D2-C025`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted) extends [`D1-C522`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D2-C025` **[Slide]** In Google's example fetch record, the robots policies that apply to a fetch, shown as the value opt-out-google-extended, travel with the fetched page into processing.
  - `D1-C522` **[Stage]** Google said a site can keep a directory or the whole site out of Gemini model training by disallowing it for the Google-Extended token in robots.txt, and that Google respects that policy; the speaker believed Google was the first to offer such an opt-out from model training.
- [`D2-C026`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted) extends [`D1-C036`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C026` **[Slide]** A Google pipeline slide placed processing between the crawler and the index and listed six processing steps: HTML parsing, rendering, deduplication, feature extraction, signal extraction and index selection.
  - `D1-C036` **[Slide]** Search runs as three stages, crawling, indexing and serving, and the event covered one stage per day.
- [`D2-C026`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted) extends [`D1-C063`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D2-C026` **[Slide]** A Google pipeline slide placed processing between the crawler and the index and listed six processing steps: HTML parsing, rendering, deduplication, feature extraction, signal extraction and index selection.
  - `D1-C063` **[Slide]** The crawl pipeline runs from a crawl queue to a scheduler to the crawler, which fetches from the internet and passes the fetch reply to indexing.
- [`D2-C031`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted) extends [`D1-C128`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) (annotates Day 1, session not recorded)
  - `D2-C031` **[Slide]** Google extracts the rel=canonical link, through which site owners state their preferred canonical URL, and uses it in deduplication and in canonical selection.
  - `D1-C128` **[Docs]** Google's canonicalization guide says some duplicate content on a site is normal and not a violation of its spam policies; Google clusters duplicate pages, picks the most representative one as canonical and crawls the duplicates less often.
- [`D2-C038`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted) extends [`D1-C040`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C038` **[Stage]** Google uses the links it extracts for three purposes: discovering new pages, determining a site's structure, and ranking.
  - `D1-C040` **[Slide]** URL discovery works through links: a homepage links to section pages, which link to further pages.
- [`D2-C048`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted) extends [`D1-C063`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D2-C048` **[Slide]** Links extracted during processing are sent back to the crawl queue, where scheduling starts again for the newly found URLs.
  - `D1-C063` **[Slide]** The crawl pipeline runs from a crawl queue to a scheduler to the crawler, which fetches from the internet and passes the fetch reply to indexing.
- [`D2-C058`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (Day 2, Controlling indexing) extends [`D1-C110`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C058` **[Stage]** John Mueller said robots.txt does not control indexing, so robots meta tags are what site owners have to use to control it.
  - `D1-C110` **[Analysis]** A URL blocked in robots.txt can still be indexed without its content if other pages link to it, and Google cannot see a noindex on a page it is not allowed to fetch.
- [`D2-C821`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (Day 2, Controlling indexing) extends [`D2-C063`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (Day 2, Controlling indexing)
  - `D2-C821` **[Stage]** John Mueller suspected that if robots meta tags were reinvented today, the page-level nofollow rule would probably not be part of them.
  - `D2-C063` **[Stage]** The page-level nofollow robots rule tells search engines not to pass signals to any of the links on the page, which John Mueller called a weird and very broad rule that makes the page stand on its own.
- [`D2-C067`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing) extends [`D1-C127`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C067` **[Analysis]** nofollow is a link-graph hint for search engines, not an access control: to keep AI crawlers away from content, use robots.txt rules for the specific crawlers; at Google, Google-Extended covers Gemini training and grounding, and the Search generative AI control covers AI Overviews and AI Mode.
  - `D1-C127` **[Docs]** Google treats nofollow as a hint for crawling, not a block: nofollow links will generally not be followed, but the linked pages may still be crawled if Google finds them through sitemaps or other links. To stop Google fetching URLs on your own site, use a robots.txt disallow rule.
- [`D2-C067`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing) extends [`D1-C482`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D2-C067` **[Analysis]** nofollow is a link-graph hint for search engines, not an access control: to keep AI crawlers away from content, use robots.txt rules for the specific crawlers; at Google, Google-Extended covers Gemini training and grounding, and the Search generative AI control covers AI Overviews and AI Mode.
  - `D1-C482` **[Stage]** Nearly all mainstream AI crawlers and AI systems use their own user agents, so robots.txt can set a separate policy for each; at the event OpenAI was said to have three or four, Anthropic a few and Microsoft some.
- [`D2-C069`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing) extends [`D1-C106`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C069` **[Docs]** Google's robots meta tag specification says robots meta tags and X-Robots-Tag headers are found only when a URL is crawled, so the rules on a URL disallowed in robots.txt are never seen and are ignored.
  - `D1-C106` **[Slide]** The noindex rule consumes crawl budget, because Google must fetch the page to see it.
- [`D2-C072`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (Day 2, Controlling indexing) extends [`D1-C034`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) (annotates Day 1, What's new in the world of Search)
  - `D2-C072` **[Slide]** The nosnippet rule also prevents a page's content from being used as a direct input for AI Overviews and AI Mode in Search.
  - `D1-C034` **[Analysis]** Lead-generation, local-service and e-commerce sites should normally stay included, because AI answers cite and link sources. Sites selling paywalled or licensed content should test exclusion on a child property first. Use nosnippet only if you also want out of regular snippets.
- [`D2-C073`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (Day 2, Controlling indexing) extends [`D1-C038`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C073` **[Stage]** John Mueller said Google uses the snippet as a way of building AI Overviews and AI Mode answers, so if a page forbids a snippet, Google cannot use that snippet for them.
  - `D1-C038` **[Slide]** AI Mode and AI Overviews use the same crawling and the same index as Search. At serving they add grounding on the Search index and query fan-out.
- [`D2-C074`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing) extends [`D1-C038`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C074` **[Docs]** Google's AI features guide says a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown in Google Search with a snippet to appear as a supporting link in AI Overviews or AI Mode, with no additional technical requirements.
  - `D1-C038` **[Slide]** AI Mode and AI Overviews use the same crawling and the same index as Search. At serving they add grounding on the Search index and query fan-out.
- [`D2-C103`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (Day 2, Controlling indexing) extends [`D1-C029`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) (Day 1, What's new in the world of Search)
  - `D2-C103` **[Slide]** Setting the Search generative AI control in Search Console to exclude keeps a site's links and content out of Search generative AI features such as AI Overviews and AI Mode, so the site gets no traffic or impressions from them; include is the default.
  - `D1-C029` **[Slide]** Search Console has a property setting called Search generative AI that gives direct control over AI Overviews and AI Mode without affecting web rankings. Its states are inherit from parent, include and exclude.
- [`D2-C852`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (Day 2, Controlling indexing) extends [`D2-C108`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (Day 2, Controlling indexing)
  - `D2-C852` **[Stage]** When Google finds a noindex rule in a page's HTML, it drops the page without even processing its JavaScript, so a script cannot switch the page back to indexable, John Mueller said.
  - `D2-C108` **[Slide]** Removing a robots restriction such as noindex with JavaScript does not work, a slide said.
- [`D2-C853`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (Day 2, Controlling indexing) extends [`D2-C106`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (Day 2, Controlling indexing)
  - `D2-C853` **[Stage]** John Mueller recommended putting robots meta tags directly in a page's HTML exactly as intended, and adding them with JavaScript only where that is not possible, as in a JavaScript web app.
  - `D2-C106` **[Slide]** A slide said robots meta rules can be added to a page's HTML with JavaScript, but doing so takes more time.
- [`D2-C855`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing) extends [`D2-C109`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing)
  - `D2-C855` **[Analysis]** On stage the rule was absolute (Google won't even process the JavaScript of a page served with noindex), while Google's guide says only that it may skip rendering; either way, a noindex in the served HTML must never be one that JavaScript is expected to lift.
  - `D2-C109` **[Analysis]** Ship robots rules in the HTML the server sends and never rely on JavaScript to lift a noindex: Google may skip rendering a page that arrives with noindex, so the page can stay out of the index even if a script removes the tag later.
- [`D2-C118`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C039`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C118` **[Stage]** To train Gemini models, Google renders every page just as it does for Search, so a page that renders correctly for Search also works for Gemini training, provided the site allows its content to be used for training.
  - `D1-C039` **[Slide]** Gemini is not part of Search, but it uses crawlers for data, shares some technologies such as tokenization and deduping, and grounds on the Search index.
- [`D2-C120`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C039`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C120` **[Stage]** When a Gemini user asks about a specific web page (for example, whether it says anything about the ruby HTML tag), the page is read at that moment rather than during crawling and may be used to ground the answer, which takes extra time.
  - `D1-C039` **[Slide]** Gemini is not part of Search, but it uses crawlers for data, shares some technologies such as tokenization and deduping, and grounds on the Search index.
- [`D2-C121`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C086`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D2-C121` **[Docs]** Google's crawler documentation defines grounding in Gemini Apps and in Grounding with Google Search on Vertex AI as providing content from the Google Search index to the model at prompt time, and sites manage whether their content is used for it with the Google-Extended robots.txt token.
  - `D1-C086` **[Docs]** Google-Extended is a control token, not a crawler with its own user agent string. It decides whether crawled content may be used to train future Gemini models and to ground Gemini apps and Vertex AI.
- [`D2-C122`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C434`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D2-C122` **[Docs]** Google says user-triggered fetchers, which fetch a URL because a user asked for it in a Google product (for example Gemini Notebook fetching URLs users add as sources, or Google-Agent acting on a user's request), generally ignore robots.txt rules.
  - `D1-C434` **[Stage]** User-initiated fetchers, such as a translation service fetching a page a user asked to translate, are a different category from crawlers and generally do not check robots.txt, because a user asked for the fetch.
- [`D2-C124`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C056`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C124` **[Stage]** Google's simple solution for the extra time of live page reads is to make JavaScript-generated content render quickly and efficiently, or to use server-side rendering.
  - `D1-C056` **[Slide]** Myth: your website is no longer relevant. Google's answer: keep content crawlable, well structured, fast and easy to read, for readers and for AI tools.
- [`D2-C127`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C063`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D2-C127` **[Slide]** A Google pipeline diagram ran from the crawl queue to the crawler, then through HTML parsing to processing, which passes pages to rendering and gets them back, and then to the index; rendering fetches its JavaScript and CSS through the crawler.
  - `D1-C063` **[Slide]** The crawl pipeline runs from a crawl queue to a scheduler to the crawler, which fetches from the internet and passes the fetch reply to indexing.
- [`D2-C128`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D2-C026`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted)
  - `D2-C128` **[Stage]** Although Google's pipeline diagram shows rendering as part of indexing, Google's rendering is a detached system, kept separate because rendering is time-consuming and computationally expensive.
  - `D2-C026` **[Slide]** A Google pipeline slide placed processing between the crawler and the index and listed six processing steps: HTML parsing, rendering, deduplication, feature extraction, signal extraction and index selection.
- [`D2-C134`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C056`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C134` **[Stage]** Google urged sites to make sure their JavaScript content can be crawled, rendered and indexed, calling this important today and also tomorrow, as AI systems increasingly ground answers to user requests.
  - `D1-C056` **[Slide]** Myth: your website is no longer relevant. Google's answer: keep content crawlable, well structured, fast and easy to read, for readers and for AI tools.
- [`D2-C136`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C121`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) (Day 1, session not recorded)
  - `D2-C136` **[Stage]** Many SEOs still treat everything beyond the raw HTML as the developers' business, but developers often do not handle rendering problems, a community speaker warned.
  - `D1-C121` **[Stage]** SEO is not only content; it has many parts.
- [`D2-C139`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C056`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C139` **[Stage]** A community speaker strongly advised putting everything you want cited into the raw, server-side rendered HTML, especially for AI systems that cannot render JavaScript yet.
  - `D1-C056` **[Slide]** Myth: your website is no longer relevant. Google's answer: keep content crawlable, well structured, fast and easy to read, for readers and for AI tools.
- [`D2-C167`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C063`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D2-C167` **[Slide]** The diagram from Google's JavaScript SEO basics page shows a URL going from the crawl queue to the crawler, the crawled HTML going to processing, then the render queue and the renderer, whose rendered HTML returns to processing before the page reaches the index.
  - `D1-C063` **[Slide]** The crawl pipeline runs from a crawl queue to a scheduler to the crawler, which fetches from the internet and passes the fetch reply to indexing.
- [`D2-C168`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C040`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C168` **[Slide]** In Google's processing step, links are extracted from the HTML Google already has, before rendering, and the URLs found go back to the crawl queue.
  - `D1-C040` **[Slide]** URL discovery works through links: a homepage links to section pages, which link to further pages.
- [`D2-C168`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D2-C048`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted)
  - `D2-C168` **[Slide]** In Google's processing step, links are extracted from the HTML Google already has, before rendering, and the URLs found go back to the crawl queue.
  - `D2-C048` **[Slide]** Links extracted during processing are sent back to the crawl queue, where scheduling starts again for the newly found URLs.
- [`D2-C169`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C040`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C169` **[Docs]** Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says Googlebot extracts links twice, from the HTML response before rendering and again from the rendered HTML, so links injected with JavaScript can be found if they use crawlable `<a href>` markup.
  - `D1-C040` **[Slide]** URL discovery works through links: a homepage links to section pages, which link to further pages.
- [`D2-C173`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C206`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C173` **[Stage]** Google's renderer is a headless Chromium that runs the page's JavaScript.
  - `D1-C206` **[Stage]** Google renders JavaScript-heavy pages from their HTML, CSS and JavaScript as a browser would, using the latest version of Chromium.
- [`D2-C184`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C115`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) (annotates Day 1, session not recorded)
  - `D2-C184` **[Slide]** Google follows links in `<a href>` elements; a link that only runs an onclick handler, or a hash pseudo-link such as href=#/products, may be invisible to Google.
  - `D1-C115` **[Docs]** Google's crawlers do not click buttons. Each page in a series needs its own URL and an `<a href>` link to the next page, should not use page 1 as its canonical, and rel=next and rel=prev are no longer used.
- [`D2-C184`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D2-C040`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted)
  - `D2-C184` **[Slide]** Google follows links in `<a href>` elements; a link that only runs an onclick handler, or a hash pseudo-link such as href=#/products, may be invisible to Google.
  - `D2-C040` **[Slide]** Google cannot extract a link from an a element that only has an onclick handler, because Googlebot does not click, so the JavaScript is never triggered.
- [`D2-C187`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C115`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) (annotates Day 1, session not recorded)
  - `D2-C187` **[Slide]** A market or language selector built as a button works for users but leaves the whole cluster of alternate-language pages without crawlable links, so the cluster is orphaned for Google.
  - `D1-C115` **[Docs]** Google's crawlers do not click buttons. Each page in a series needs its own URL and an `<a href>` link to the next page, should not use page 1 as its canonical, and rel=next and rel=prev are no longer used.
- [`D2-C188`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C101`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C188` **[Analysis]** Hash-fragment links are a problem only where Google should follow them: product, category and language links need a real URL in an `<a href>`, while fragments can deliberately keep filter combinations out of the crawl, as Google's faceted navigation guide allows.
  - `D1-C101` **[Docs]** Google's faceted navigation guide prefers prevention: disallow filter URLs in robots.txt and keep crawlable only item pages plus one unfiltered listing page, or use URL fragments, which Google generally does not crawl. rel=canonical and nofollow are weaker, slower options.
- [`D2-C189`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C067`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (annotates Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D2-C189` **[Analysis]** Build market and language selectors as plain `<a href>` links to each alternate URL, not buttons or script handlers; otherwise the language versions have no internal links and depend on sitemaps to be found, which is slow.
  - `D1-C067` **[Analysis]** A page with no internal links depends on sitemaps alone to be found, so it is discovered slowly and attracts little crawl demand.

  - `D2-C190` **[Stage]** In single-page apps, a missing page often shows a custom 404 page while the server returns HTTP 200, because the front-end router, not the server, handles the 404.
  - `D1-C073` **[Docs]** A soft 404 is a page that returns a success code while its content looks like an error or an empty page. It is kept out of the index but continues to be crawled, wasting crawl budget.

  - `D2-C195` **[Slide]** Content that loads only after a user action such as a click or a scroll is not in the DOM while Google renders the page, so Google cannot index it.
  - `D1-C115` **[Docs]** Google's crawlers do not click buttons. Each page in a series needs its own URL and an `<a href>` link to the next page, should not use page 1 as its canonical, and rel=next and rel=prev are no longer used.
- [`D2-C197`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C114`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D2-C197` **[Slide]** Lazy loading triggered by a scroll event listener, such as window.addEventListener('scroll', loadMoreProducts), never runs for Googlebot because Googlebot does not scroll.
