  - `D2-C201` **[Slide]** Tab or accordion content fetched from an API only when a user clicks the tab, as in tab.onclick = () => fetch('/api/specs'), does not exist for Google until someone clicks.
  - `D1-C115` **[Docs]** Google's crawlers do not click buttons. Each page in a series needs its own URL and an `<a href>` link to the next page, should not use page 1 as its canonical, and rel=next and rel=prev are no longer used.
- [`D2-C204`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C064`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D2-C204` **[Slide]** Blocking JavaScript or API resources in robots.txt is a classic rendering mistake: if Google's renderer cannot fetch a resource, it cannot run it.
  - `D1-C064` **[Slide]** The crawler has multiple tasks: fetch from the internet, ensure it doesn't break the internet, and enforce robots.txt policies. Fetched data is sent for indexing.
- [`D2-C208`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript) extends [`D1-C081`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D2-C208` **[Analysis]** A robots.txt carve-out works because Google applies the most specific matching rule, so Allow: /api/products/ beats Disallow: /api/ for product endpoints only; re-test a rendered page after every robots.txt change to script or API paths.
  - `D1-C081` **[Docs]** When matching rules to a URL, Google uses the most specific rule by path length. If rules conflict, it uses the least restrictive one.

- [`D2-C345`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C128`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) (annotates Day 1, session not recorded)
  - `D2-C345` **[Slide]** Google's deduplication has three steps: identify and cluster duplicate web pages, pick representative URLs and index the unique pages, and forward signals to the representative URLs.
  - `D1-C128` **[Docs]** Google's canonicalization guide says some duplicate content on a site is normal and not a violation of its spam policies; Google clusters duplicate pages, picks the most representative one as canonical and crawls the duplicates less often.

  - `D2-C345` **[Slide]** Google's deduplication has three steps: identify and cluster duplicate web pages, pick representative URLs and index the unique pages, and forward signals to the representative URLs.
  - `D1-C207` **[Stage]** Google clusters duplicate pages and selects one page per cluster as its representative, the canonical URL, so that users are not shown duplicates.
- [`D2-C346`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C207`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C346` **[Stage]** For deduplication, a cluster is a set of pages Google considers essentially equivalent: Google stores one of them in the index and keeps track of the other related URLs.
  - `D1-C207` **[Stage]** Google clusters duplicate pages and selects one page per cluster as its representative, the canonical URL, so that users are not shown duplicates.
- [`D2-C348`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C111`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) (Day 1, session not recorded)
  - `D2-C348` **[Slide]** Google forwards the signals attached to every URL in a duplicate cluster, such as links, to the representative URL, so that nothing is lost by showing only one URL.

- [`D2-C367`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C073`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (annotates Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D2-C367` **[Stage]** Soft 404 pages are another reason Google clusters pages together, an outcome site owners usually do not want.
  - `D1-C073` **[Docs]** A soft 404 is a page that returns a success code while its content looks like an error or an empty page. It is kept out of the index but continues to be crawled, wasting crawl budget.
- [`D2-C369`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C128`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) (annotates Day 1, session not recorded)
  - `D2-C369` **[Slide]** Google's slide on structurally similar content asked whether a new URL that fits a known duplicate pattern, such as /buy/seo-service, even needs to be crawled.
  - `D1-C128` **[Docs]** Google's canonicalization guide says some duplicate content on a site is normal and not a violation of its spam policies; Google clusters duplicate pages, picks the most representative one as canonical and crawls the duplicates less often.
- [`D2-C369`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C094`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C369` **[Slide]** Google's slide on structurally similar content asked whether a new URL that fits a known duplicate pattern, such as /buy/seo-service, even needs to be crawled.
  - `D1-C094` **[Slide]** If the quality or popularity of a URL is unknown, the aggregate quality or popularity of its parent path is used, then that path's parent, and so on.
- [`D2-C374`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C069`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D2-C374` **[Stage]** A growing cause of wrong clustering is bot protection: when a CDN or another protection system shows Googlebot the same 'you look like a bot, solve this puzzle' page on many unrelated URLs or domains, Google can cluster those pages as duplicates.
  - `D1-C069` **[Stage]** DNS issues and firewalls are blind spots: Google does not know a firewall is blocking it, it only sees that requests fail.
- [`D2-C374`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C078`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (annotates Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D2-C374` **[Stage]** A growing cause of wrong clustering is bot protection: when a CDN or another protection system shows Googlebot the same 'you look like a bot, solve this puzzle' page on many unrelated URLs or domains, Google can cluster those pages as duplicates.
  - `D1-C078` **[Analysis]** For temporary blocks return 503 or 429, never a 200 page with a captcha or error message, which becomes a soft 404 and can replace real content in the index. Verify Googlebot by reverse DNS, not by user agent.
- [`D2-C374`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C367`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D2-C374` **[Stage]** A growing cause of wrong clustering is bot protection: when a CDN or another protection system shows Googlebot the same 'you look like a bot, solve this puzzle' page on many unrelated URLs or domains, Google can cluster those pages as duplicates.
  - `D1-C367` **[Stage]** CDN captcha challenges often return HTTP 200; Googlebot does not solve them and sees only content with a 200 status, which indexing then classifies as a soft 404, reported as an error in Search Console.
- [`D2-C375`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C367`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D2-C375` **[Stage]** Google's systems find it very hard to recognise a bot-challenge page as an error page, and Googlebot cannot solve the puzzles, such as selecting all the cats, that those pages ask for.
  - `D1-C367` **[Stage]** CDN captcha challenges often return HTTP 200; Googlebot does not solve them and sees only content with a 200 status, which indexing then classifies as a soft 404, reported as an error in Search Console.
- [`D2-C376`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (annotates Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C078`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (annotates Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D2-C376` **[Docs]** Google's Search Central post on CDNs says that if Google cannot recognise an error message served with a 200 status as an error, all pages showing the same message may be dropped from the index as duplicates, and recovery can be slow because Google has little incentive to recrawl duplicates. For bot-verification interstitials it recommends sending crawlers a 503 status.
  - `D1-C078` **[Analysis]** For temporary blocks return 503 or 429, never a 200 page with a captcha or error message, which becomes a soft 404 and can replace real content in the index. Verify Googlebot by reverse DNS, not by user agent.
- [`D2-C377`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C436`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D2-C377` **[Stage]** AI agents that browse the web for users run into the same bot walls that sites put up against scrapers, and may give up and go to another site, for example to buy the product elsewhere.
  - `D1-C436` **[Stage]** A Google panelist argued that it makes business sense for agents not to follow robots.txt: an agent sent to buy something that obeyed a robots.txt block could not complete the purchase, a bad experience for the user and lost revenue for the shop.
- [`D2-C379`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D2-C031`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted)
  - `D2-C379` **[Stage]** rel=canonical is probably the most common way site owners signal duplicates, but it is very often wrong, for example a tag whose value reads 'canonical target' instead of a real URL (the example is partly unclear in the recording), so Google can only sometimes trust it.
  - `D2-C031` **[Slide]** Google extracts the rel=canonical link, through which site owners state their preferred canonical URL, and uses it in deduplication and in canonical selection.
- [`D2-C380`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C113`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) (annotates Day 1, session not recorded)
  - `D2-C380` **[Stage]** Many SEOs assume Google must follow their rel=canonical, but because people sometimes get it wrong, Google has to make its own judgment about the canonical.
  - `D1-C113` **[Analysis]** The real cost of duplicates is control and crawling: Google may choose a canonical you did not want, and every copy is still crawled. Copied or scraped content is a separate spam-policy issue.
- [`D2-C382`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D2-C033`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted)
  - `D2-C382` **[Slide]** When localized pages are clustered, Google tries to use hreflang alternates; the speaker's short version of the advice was to use hreflang, which he called really helpful for same-language, different-country content.
  - `D2-C033` **[Slide]** Google extracts hreflang annotations, through which site owners specify the language variants of their content, to know whether a page has an equivalent with similar content in another language.
- [`D2-C395`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (annotates Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C115`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) (annotates Day 1, session not recorded)
  - `D2-C395` **[Docs]** Google's 2013 post on rel=canonical mistakes says pointing rel=canonical from page 2 or later of a paginated series to page 1 is incorrect because the pages are not duplicates, and that it would result in the content on later pages not being indexed at all.
  - `D1-C115` **[Docs]** Google's crawlers do not click buttons. Each page in a series needs its own URL and an `<a href>` link to the next page, should not use page 1 as its canonical, and rel=next and rel=prev are no longer used.
- [`D2-C397`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) extends [`D1-C131`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) (annotates Day 1, session not recorded)
  - `D2-C397` **[Slide]** Google's duplication talk closed with the advice not to block agents, which the speaker said are sometimes really cool.
  - `D1-C131` **[Docs]** Google's guide for generative AI features says browser agents may read a site through screenshots, the DOM structure and the accessibility tree, and recommends semantic HTML because it helps users such as screen reader users navigate a page.

  - `D1-C128` **[Docs]** Google's canonicalization guide says some duplicate content on a site is normal and not a violation of its spam policies; Google clusters duplicate pages, picks the most representative one as canonical and crawls the duplicates less often.

  - `D2-C408` **[Stage]** A community speaker advised auditing canonicals as whole canonical groups rather than pair by pair, paying special attention to each group's canonical leader.

- [`D2-C427`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) (Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves) extends [`D1-C067`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (annotates Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D2-C427` **[Stage]** When internal links point only to page A and the canonical leader is reached only through A's canonical link, the leader is reachable by machines but not by human visitors, a signal conflict that asks the search engine to index a page users cannot reach.
  - `D1-C067` **[Analysis]** A page with no internal links depends on sitemaps alone to be found, so it is discovered slowly and attracts little crawl demand.
- [`D2-C873`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) (Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves) extends [`D2-C402`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) (Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves)
  - `D2-C873` **[Stage]** A community speaker said that, under the canonical link specification, an improperly declared canonical tag can also be ignored completely by the application that processes it, not only replaced by that application's own heuristic.
  - `D2-C402` **[Stage]** According to the canonical link specification cited by a community speaker, when a canonical tag is declared improperly, the application that processes it may apply its own heuristic and decide what to do instead.
- [`D2-C882`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) (Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves) extends [`D2-C396`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication)
  - `D2-C882` **[Stage]** In a community case study, an old URL got a 301 redirect only when a new page served the same intent; URLs with no same-intent match were removed with an error status instead of being redirected (the exact code is unclear in the recording).
  - `D2-C396` **[Slide]** Google's closing suggestions on duplication: use redirects for site migrations, use HTTP result codes, don't block agents, check your rel=canonical links, use hreflang links to help Google localize, report weird canonicals in the forums, make secure pages that work, and keep canonical signals clear.
- [`D2-C884`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) (Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves) extends [`D1-C540`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D2-C884` **[Stage]** The technical steps of a community speaker's domain consolidation included submitting new sitemaps, filing a change of address in Search Console and updating internal links so the new pages did not rely on redirects alone.
  - `D1-C540` **[Stage]** Asked how to plan a migration that does not leave many URLs unindexed, a Google panelist said the answer is probably not sitemaps: decide what matters from the business's perspective (for example whether to consolidate languages); listing the new URLs in a sitemap is probably a good idea and cannot hurt, but it is not the main tool.
- [`D2-C886`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) (Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves) extends [`D1-C103`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C886` **[Stage]** A community speaker listed the technical SEO goals of a two-site consolidation as lighter pages, faster loading and no crawl budget spent on content that no longer mattered.
  - `D1-C103` **[Slide]** Four ways to manage crawl budget: use HTTP cache control, have good site navigation, restrict crawlers' access to faceted navigation and action URLs, and improve or remove useless content.
- [`D2-C903`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) (Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves) extends [`D2-C334`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) (Day 2, Understanding what's on a page)
  - `D2-C903` **[Stage]** A community speaker warned that HTTP 200 responses across a new domain show only that the URLs work, not that the content users came for is still there, so after launch the redirect map becomes the test.
  - `D2-C334` **[Stage]** A soft 404 is a page that should return an error status code but returns HTTP 200; from a crawling point of view it looks indexable, but because it has no real content Google throws it out of the index.
- [`D2-C441`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S11-finding-the-gold-nuggets-structured-data-media-and-more.md) (Day 2, Finding the gold nuggets: structured data, media, and more!) extends [`D1-C063`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D2-C441` **[Slide]** Google's indexing pipeline slide put a Processing stage between the crawler and the index and listed HTML parsing, rendering, deduplication and feature extraction above it, with feature extraction highlighted as the step of this talk.
  - `D1-C063` **[Slide]** The crawl pipeline runs from a crawl queue to a scheduler to the crawler, which fetches from the internet and passes the fetch reply to indexing.
- [`D2-C444`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S11-finding-the-gold-nuggets-structured-data-media-and-more.md) (Day 2, Finding the gold nuggets: structured data, media, and more!) extends [`D2-C026`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted)
  - `D2-C444` **[Stage]** Google runs deduplication before feature extraction, so that the expensive extraction work is spent only on a trimmed-down, manageable set of documents.
  - `D2-C026` **[Slide]** A Google pipeline slide placed processing between the crawler and the index and listed six processing steps: HTML parsing, rendering, deduplication, feature extraction, signal extraction and index selection.

  - `D2-C452` **[Stage]** Search results have moved from ten blue links to feature-rich, media-rich results because users wanted more.

  - `D2-C452` **[Stage]** Search results have moved from ten blue links to feature-rich, media-rich results because users wanted more.

  - `D2-C462` **[Docs]** Google's guidance on generative AI content warns that AI output can contain hallucinations and says AI-generated metadata, including structured data and image alt text, should be fact-checked before publishing and the markup validated.

- [`D2-C465`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) (Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet.) extends [`D1-C131`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) (annotates Day 1, session not recorded)
  - `D2-C465` **[Stage]** Gemini in Chrome relies heavily on the screenshot it takes of a page.
  - `D1-C131` **[Docs]** Google's guide for generative AI features says browser agents may read a site through screenshots, the DOM structure and the accessibility tree, and recommends semantic HTML because it helps users such as screen reader users navigate a page.
- [`D2-C474`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) (Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet.) extends [`D2-C028`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted)
  - `D2-C474` **[Stage]** Google's systems sometimes fail to determine a page's main content correctly, and structured data helps because site owners tend to mark up what is actually important rather than boilerplate or ads.

- [`D2-C612`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) (annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation) extends [`D1-C048`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (annotates Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)

- [`D2-C648`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) (Day 2, Calculating (some) signals) extends [`D1-C037`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)

  - `D1-C037` **[Slide]** For classic Search, crawling means Googlebot, scheduling and robots.txt, with AI used in parts such as scheduling. Indexing is one big but not limitless index that calculates signals and understands more than words, with AI such as BERT. Serving uses hundreds of signals tailored to the moment, with AI such as RankBrain.
- [`D2-C651`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) (Day 2, Calculating (some) signals) extends [`D2-C585`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) (Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation)
  - `D2-C651` **[Stage]** Google detects the language of each document and weights language in index selection so that the index is not dominated by one or two languages.

- [`D2-C656`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) (Day 2, Calculating (some) signals) extends [`D1-C045`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C656` **[Stage]** Freshness is a signal for queries that deserve fresh results ('query deserves freshness'): when a breaking event hits a city, such as possible closure of Barcelona's airport, users want really fresh results, not results from two weeks ago.
  - `D1-C045` **[Slide]** Ranking signals differ by result type: web pages (text, links, passages), images (resolution, colour, associated text), news (freshness, originality, diversity), local (location, type, rating, reviews, hours) and videos (language, text from speech).
- [`D2-C668`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) (Day 2, Calculating (some) signals) extends [`D1-C041`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C668` **[Stage]** Google uses more and more AI to detect spam, and Google's testing shows that this AI-based detection is highly accurate.
  - `D1-C041` **[Slide]** Statistical models have been used at Google for over 20 years, for catching spam and originally for the 'Did you mean' feature.
- [`D2-C669`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) (Day 2, Calculating (some) signals) extends [`D1-C041`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C669` **[Stage]** SpamBrain, Google's AI-based spam detection system, is nowadays built on Gemini and fine-tuned specifically for finding spam.
  - `D1-C041` **[Slide]** Statistical models have been used at Google for over 20 years, for catching spam and originally for the 'Did you mean' feature.
- [`D2-C669`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) (Day 2, Calculating (some) signals) extends [`D1-C039`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C669` **[Stage]** SpamBrain, Google's AI-based spam detection system, is nowadays built on Gemini and fine-tuned specifically for finding spam.
  - `D1-C039` **[Slide]** Gemini is not part of Search, but it uses crawlers for data, shares some technologies such as tokenization and deduping, and grounds on the Search index.
- [`D2-C682`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C211`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C682` **[Stage]** Google's index selection system calculates thresholds and decides which documents are kept and which are thrown out; a URL that does not meet the thresholds is not indexed.
  - `D1-C211` **[Stage]** Index selection runs after signals are collected and duplicates are dropped, and decides what goes into Google's index, which is big but not limitless.
- [`D2-C684`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C037`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C684` **[Stage]** Index selection is a predictive AI system that relies heavily on machine learning.
  - `D1-C037` **[Slide]** For classic Search, crawling means Googlebot, scheduling and robots.txt, with AI used in parts such as scheduling. Indexing is one big but not limitless index that calculates signals and understands more than words, with AI such as BERT. Serving uses hundreds of signals tailored to the moment, with AI such as RankBrain.
- [`D2-C685`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C094`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C685` **[Stage]** Index selection uses what Google already knows about a site: if the site, or even a section of it, satisfies users' needs well, new URLs from it are treated more forgivingly.
  - `D1-C094` **[Slide]** If the quality or popularity of a URL is unknown, the aggregate quality or popularity of its parent path is used, then that path's parent, and so on.
- [`D2-C686`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C095`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C686` **[Analysis]** Launch new pages under sections that Google already indexes well, and improve or remove weak sections, because index selection judges new URLs partly by what it knows about the site and the section they sit in.
  - `D1-C095` **[Analysis]** New content inherits its starting crawl demand from the folder it sits in. Put new high-value content under sections Google already rates well, not under weak ones.
- [`D2-C687`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C205`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C687` **[Stage]** Index selection uses the signals calculated earlier in indexing for each document it has to select or discard.
  - `D1-C205` **[Stage]** Signals calculated for a page during indexing are stored in the index and used both to decide whether the page gets indexed and, later, for ranking.
- [`D2-C688`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D2-C026`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) (Day 2, How is HTML interpreted)
  - `D2-C688` **[Stage]** Index selection is the last step before documents enter Google's index.
  - `D2-C026` **[Slide]** A Google pipeline slide placed processing between the crawler and the index and listed six processing steps: HTML parsing, rendering, deduplication, feature extraction, signal extraction and index selection.
- [`D2-C688`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C211`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C688` **[Stage]** Index selection is the last step before documents enter Google's index.
  - `D1-C211` **[Stage]** Index selection runs after signals are collected and duplicates are dropped, and decides what goes into Google's index, which is big but not limitless.
- [`D2-C695`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C093`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C695` **[Stage]** Page quality is ultimately what decides whether a document is indexed, so focusing on quality is the most reliable way to get pages into Google's index.
  - `D1-C093` **[Slide]** Crawl demand is driven by the quality of the site, the change frequency of its URLs and their popularity on the internet.
- [`D2-C697`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C106`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C697` **[Stage]** Index selection drops a document carrying a noindex rule if it was not already dropped earlier in processing (noindex is a likely but not certain reading of the transcript, supported by the later mention of noindex among the Page indexing report reasons).
  - `D1-C106` **[Slide]** The noindex rule consumes crawl budget, because Google must fetch the page to see it.
- [`D2-C698`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D2-C100`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (Day 2, Controlling indexing)
  - `D2-C698` **[Stage]** Index selection checks for the robots unavailable_after rule and its date, and drops a page from the index once that date is reached.
  - `D2-C100` **[Stage]** The unavailable_after rule lets a page drop out of search results after a set date and time, which suits time-bound pages, though John Mueller said most sites do not use it.
- [`D2-C700`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C073`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (annotates Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D2-C700` **[Stage]** Index selection drops soft 404 pages that were not dropped earlier, for example when a document is reprocessed.
  - `D1-C073` **[Docs]** A soft 404 is a page that returns a success code while its content looks like an error or an empty page. It is kept out of the index but continues to be crawled, wasting crawl budget.
- [`D2-C700`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D2-C334`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) (Day 2, Understanding what's on a page)
  - `D2-C700` **[Stage]** Index selection drops soft 404 pages that were not dropped earlier, for example when a document is reprocessed.
  - `D2-C334` **[Stage]** A soft 404 is a page that should return an error status code but returns HTTP 200; from a crawling point of view it looks indexable, but because it has no real content Google throws it out of the index.
- [`D2-C701`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C128`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) (annotates Day 1, session not recorded)
  - `D2-C701` **[Stage]** When Google already has duplicate information for a document, for example when reprocessing it, index selection uses it to drop non-canonical duplicates from further processing, so that, as the speaker put it, only canonicals end up in search results (a simplification; see D2-C703).
  - `D1-C128` **[Docs]** Google's canonicalization guide says some duplicate content on a site is normal and not a violation of its spam policies; Google clusters duplicate pages, picks the most representative one as canonical and crawls the duplicates less often.
- [`D2-C701`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D2-C345`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication)
  - `D2-C701` **[Stage]** When Google already has duplicate information for a document, for example when reprocessing it, index selection uses it to drop non-canonical duplicates from further processing, so that, as the speaker put it, only canonicals end up in search results (a simplification; see D2-C703).
  - `D2-C345` **[Slide]** Google's deduplication has three steps: identify and cluster duplicate web pages, pick representative URLs and index the unique pages, and forward signals to the representative URLs.
- [`D2-C706`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C097`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C706` **[Stage]** 'Discovered – currently not indexed' in Search Console is a crawl-scheduling state: Google knows the URL exists but does not want to crawl it yet. Of the two not-indexed statuses discussed, it was called the 'kind of nastier' one.
  - `D1-C097` **[Docs]** Google's crawl budget guide is written for sites with over 1 million unique pages that change weekly, over 10,000 pages that change daily, or many URLs reported as 'Discovered – currently not indexed'.
- [`D2-C706`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C065`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D2-C706` **[Stage]** 'Discovered – currently not indexed' in Search Console is a crawl-scheduling state: Google knows the URL exists but does not want to crawl it yet. Of the two not-indexed statuses discussed, it was called the 'kind of nastier' one.
  - `D1-C065` **[Slide]** The scheduler is shared infrastructure that decides what to fetch and when and sends URLs to the crawler. Each team decides the scheduling parameters for its own user agents.
- [`D2-C708`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C098`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C708` **[Analysis]** The help page explains 'Discovered – currently not indexed' by expected server overload (capacity), while on stage it was explained as Google not wanting the URL yet (demand); the crawl budget guide covers both, so first rule out slow responses and server errors, then treat the status as a quality and demand problem.
  - `D1-C098` **[Analysis]** On smaller sites, slow indexing is almost always a demand problem, meaning quality, not a capacity problem.
- [`D2-C709`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C093`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C709` **[Stage]** Site owners can influence 'Discovered – currently not indexed' by getting other URLs of the site indexed and showing Google's systems that the site's content is good and useful to users.
  - `D1-C093` **[Slide]** Crawl demand is driven by the quality of the site, the change frequency of its URLs and their popularity on the internet.
- [`D2-C714`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C098`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C714` **[Stage]** 'Crawled – currently not indexed' is most of the time a quality issue rather than a technical one: the pages are usually low quality or useless for the index, for example duplicates or soft 404s.
  - `D1-C098` **[Analysis]** On smaller sites, slow indexing is almost always a demand problem, meaning quality, not a capacity problem.
- [`D2-C716`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C098`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D2-C716` **[Analysis]** Treat 'Crawled – currently not indexed' as a quality audit list: compare those URLs with indexed pages of the same type for thin, duplicate or soft-404-like content and for template differences before looking for technical faults.
  - `D1-C098` **[Analysis]** On smaller sites, slow indexing is almost always a demand problem, meaning quality, not a capacity problem.
- [`D2-C717`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) (Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?) extends [`D1-C368`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)

Serving uses hundreds of signals tailored to the moment, with AI such as RankBrain.

  - `D2-C321` **[Stage]** For languages written without spaces, such as Thai and Chinese, Google uses exactly the same word segmentation when indexing a page as when interpreting the user's query, because otherwise the query could not be matched against the index.

  - `D3-C013` **[Stage]** Google's query processing deliberately mirrors indexing: a query is transformed into something that can be matched against the index, and stop word removal is part of that transformation.

  - `D3-C075` **[Stage]** At retrieval, Google splits the query into words, applies query understanding and expansion, and matches the words and their expansions against the posting lists.
  - `D2-C738` **[Stage]** At retrieval, Google looks up the posting lists of the query words that are actually important rather than of every word in the query.
- [`D3-C077`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) (Day 3, Making sense of users' queries) extends [`D2-C740`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) (Day 2, How does the index look like?)
  - `D3-C077` **[Stage]** The first condition for retrieving a document is that the query's words, or its concepts in the case of vectors or embeddings, are in the document or related to it.
  - `D2-C740` **[Stage]** Besides posting lists, Google can retrieve documents through vector embeddings: parts of documents are associated with embeddings, which form a vector space used for retrieval.
- [`D3-C079`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) (Day 3, Making sense of users' queries) extends [`D2-C722`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) (Day 2, How does the index look like?)
  - `D3-C079` **[Stage]** To order candidates at retrieval, Google uses signals collected during indexing, and the first two are language and country.
  - `D2-C722` **[Stage]** Each document in Google's index has pretty much all the signals calculated for it attached, for example quality signals plus the page's country and language, according to an illustration the speaker called an approximation of the real structure.
- [`D3-C079`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) (Day 3, Making sense of users' queries) extends [`D2-C649`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) (Day 2, Calculating (some) signals)
  - `D3-C079` **[Stage]** To order candidates at retrieval, Google uses signals collected during indexing, and the first two are language and country.
  - `D2-C649` **[Stage]** Country and language are among Google's most important signals and have been used since Google's early days.
- [`D3-C080`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) (Day 3, Making sense of users' queries) extends [`D2-C654`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) (Day 2, Calculating (some) signals)
  - `D3-C080` **[Stage]** At retrieval, Google tries to match results to the user's language wherever possible: someone searching in Spanish does not necessarily want results in Italian.
  - `D2-C654` **[Stage]** In ranking, country and language signals help Google serve users the right content for their country and language.
- [`D3-C082`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) (Day 3, Making sense of users' queries) extends [`D2-C649`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) (Day 2, Calculating (some) signals)
  - `D3-C082` **[Stage]** Country is the second retrieval signal: a user searching from Switzerland wants cheese from Switzerland, not from Germany, and a user in Spain is poorly served by results targeting a South American country.
  - `D2-C649` **[Stage]** Country and language are among Google's most important signals and have been used since Google's early days.
- [`D3-C083`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) (Day 3, Making sense of users' queries) extends [`D2-C722`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) (Day 2, How does the index look like?)
  - `D3-C083` **[Stage]** Google called quality the most important of the signals used to order candidates at retrieval: a URL of high quality is more likely to be retrieved from the index for specific queries.
  - `D2-C722` **[Stage]** Each document in Google's index has pretty much all the signals calculated for it attached, for example quality signals plus the page's country and language, according to an illustration the speaker called an approximation of the real structure.
- [`D3-C104`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) (Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality) extends [`D2-C789`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) (Day 2, Google Trends)
  - `D3-C104` **[Stage]** To choose what to cover in depth, a community speaker's team used Google Trends to find what people in their market were interested in and then gave them that content.
  - `D2-C789` **[Stage]** Google presented three uses of Google Trends for content creation, marketing and SEO: keyword selection, scheduling and ideation.
- [`D3-C109`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) (annotates Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality) extends [`D2-C318`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) (Day 2, Understanding what's on a page)
  - `D3-C109` **[Analysis]** The inspector metaphor blends two steps: Googlebot fetches pages during crawling, while tokenization happens later when the page is processed for the index, as Google explained on Day 2.
  - `D2-C318` **[Stage]** Google does not store the complete sentences or the full HTML of a page in the Search index, because large pieces of text would be unsearchable; it tokenizes the text into the smallest segments that still allow search.
- [`D3-C131`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) (Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality) extends [`D3-C084`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) (Day 3, Making sense of users' queries)
  - `D3-C131` **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said quality is one of the most important ranking signals, although Google uses hundreds of ranking signals (the word 'quality' is a repaired speech-to-text reading).
  - `D3-C084` **[Stage]** The same quality signal that Google uses at retrieval is also used in ranking when results are served.
- [`D3-C135`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) (annotates Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality) extends [`D1-C130`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (annotates Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D3-C135` **[Analysis]** The quality talk's slide listed MUM among Google's ranking systems, while Google's ranking systems guide says MUM is not currently used for general ranking in Search; read the slide as a list of systems Google runs, not as proof that each one ranks every query.
  - `D1-C130` **[Docs]** Google's ranking systems guide says MUM is not currently used for general ranking in Search, only for specific applications such as COVID-19 vaccine searches and featured snippet callouts.
- [`D3-C147`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) (Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality) extends [`D1-C158`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) (Day 1, Welcome and opening keynotes)
  - `D3-C147` **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said that at any moment thousands of Search experiments are probably running.
  - `D1-C158` **[Stage]** Google said that even the classic ten-blue-links layout was settled only after millions of experiments, as part of using as much data as possible for product decisions.
- [`D3-C170`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) (Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality) extends [`D2-C311`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) (Day 2, Understanding what's on a page)
  - `D3-C170` **[Stage]** Google's quality talk pointed to page 21 of the Search Quality Rater Guidelines for its definition of content quality by effort, originality, talent or skill and accuracy, noting that the document is updated from time to time.
  - `D2-C311` **[Stage]** Gary Illyes pointed to Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines as the detailed source on how Google thinks about the main content of a page.
- [`D3-C179`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) (Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality) extends [`D1-C055`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D3-C179` **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said non-commodity content offers a unique, experienced take, and advised writing content that readers will find very helpful and reliable.
  - `D1-C055` **[Slide]** Myth: build content for every possible consumer need. Google's answer: prioritise unique perspectives, expertise and in-depth experience that go beyond common knowledge.
- [`D3-C205`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) (Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality) extends [`D2-C668`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) (Day 2, Calculating (some) signals)
  - `D3-C205` **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said AI has fundamentally changed how Google builds spam updates, letting it evaluate many more candidates and drastically increasing its velocity, so it launches faster with more impact.
  - `D2-C668` **[Stage]** Google uses more and more AI to detect spam, and Google's testing shows that this AI-based detection is highly accurate.
- [`D3-C206`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) (Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality) extends [`D2-C668`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) (Day 2, Calculating (some) signals)
  - `D3-C206` **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said AI lets Google catch new types of spam and catch more of it.
  - `D2-C668` **[Stage]** Google uses more and more AI to detect spam, and Google's testing shows that this AI-based detection is highly accurate.
- [`D3-C212`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) (Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality) extends [`D1-C129`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (annotates Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D3-C212` **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said Google clarified that traditional spam techniques aimed at manipulating AI responses also violate its spam policies, and that Google can take action against them.
  - `D1-C129` **[Docs]** Google's guide says creating separate content for every variation of how people might search, including fan-out queries, primarily to manipulate rankings or AI responses violates its scaled content abuse policy. It adds that its AI systems can understand a page's relevance even without an exact match to the query.
- [`D3-C224`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) (Day 3, Uncovering Trustworthy Experiences on Discover) extends [`D2-C089`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) (Day 2, Controlling indexing)
  - `D3-C224` **[Slide]** Google's Discover slide recommended large images at least 1,200 px wide, with more than 300,000 total pixels and a 16x9 aspect ratio, enabled by the max-image-preview:large setting.
  - `D2-C089` **[Stage]** max-image-preview:large matters mainly in Discover, where it allows a large image that draws people's attention, so the rule can make a page more visible than leaving it out, John Mueller said.
- [`D3-C239`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) (Day 3, What are quality updates) extends [`D3-C197`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) (Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality)
  - `D3-C239` **[Slide]** Google's slide, headed 'In 2023, there were...', said 40 billion spammy pages are detected every day.
  - `D3-C197` **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said Google discovers tens of billions of spam pages every day.
- [`D3-C265`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) (Day 3, What are quality updates) extends [`D3-C170`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) (Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality)
  - `D3-C265` **[Stage]** Google sometimes couples a core update with an update to its Search Quality Rater Guidelines.
  - `D3-C170` **[Stage]** Google's quality talk pointed to page 21 of the Search Quality Rater Guidelines for its definition of content quality by effort, originality, talent or skill and accuracy, noting that the document is updated from time to time.
- [`D3-C284`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) (Day 3, What are quality updates) extends [`D3-C207`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) (Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality)
  - `D3-C284` **[Stage]** Reviewing the spam slide, the speaker said link spam would probably be replaced with scaled content abuse as the spam type worth talking about today.
  - `D3-C207` **[Stage]** Google's quality talk listed recent updates to Google's spam policies: back button hijacking, scaled content abuse and manipulating AI responses.
- [`D3-C287`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) (annotates Day 3, What are quality updates) extends [`D2-C670`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) (Day 2, Calculating (some) signals)
  - `D3-C287` **[Docs]** Google's spam updates page says its automated spam detection systems run constantly, and a notable improvement to them, such as to the AI-based SpamBrain system, is called a spam update and listed with Google's ranking updates.
  - `D2-C670` **[Stage]** SpamBrain is central to Google's spam-fighting efforts and has been improved many times since its launch.
- [`D3-C304`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) (Day 3, How Search results are born) extends [`D3-C004`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) (Day 3, Making sense of users' queries)
  - `D3-C304` **[Stage]** Which kinds of results Google shows for a query is decided by query understanding, which tries to predict the intent behind the query.
  - `D3-C004` **[Stage]** Google placed query understanding in the traditional part of Search, the part where answers are looked up in an index and then presented and ranked.
- [`D3-C311`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) (Day 3, How Search results are born) extends [`D2-C740`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) (Day 2, How does the index look like?)
  - `D3-C311` **[Stage]** Google handles an image used as a search query much like a text query interpreted as an embedding: the image is broken down into vectors (embeddings) that are then searched for in the index.
  - `D2-C740` **[Stage]** Besides posting lists, Google can retrieve documents through vector embeddings: parts of documents are associated with embeddings, which form a vector space used for retrieval.
- [`D3-C316`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) (Day 3, How Search results are born) extends [`D2-C724`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) (Day 2, How does the index look like?)
  - `D3-C316` **[Stage]** Google generates the parts of a text result, such as title link and snippet, from its understanding of the underlying web page, even when the site owner provides nothing extra.
  - `D2-C724` **[Stage]** The snippet shown for a web result is reconstructed from the tokens stored in Google's index: Google knows the position of each token in the document and rebuilds the snippet from those positions.
- [`D3-C317`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) (Day 3, How Search results are born) extends [`D1-C027`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) (Day 1, What's new in the world of Search)
  - `D3-C317` **[Stage]** Google can add elements to a text result, such as a 'highly cited' badge or a preferred-source badge.
  - `D1-C027` **[Slide]** Sites that users mark as a preferred source are more visible in Top Stories and are labelled in AI Mode and AI Overviews.
- [`D3-C319`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) (Day 3, How Search results are born) extends [`D2-C525`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) (Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos)
  - `D3-C319` **[Stage]** Image results shown among web results come from Google's image index and are roughly the same images that Google Images shows for the same query.
  - `D2-C525` **[Stage]** An image Google has extracted can appear almost anywhere Google shows results, including Discover, image search, web search and AI features, so its potential reach is immense.
- [`D3-C323`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) (Day 3, How Search results are born) extends [`D2-C446`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S11-finding-the-gold-nuggets-structured-data-media-and-more.md) (Day 2, Finding the gold nuggets: structured data, media, and more!)
  - `D3-C323` **[Stage]** Most of Google's search features need nothing extra from the site owner; Google generates them from what it extracted from the page during indexing.
  - `D2-C446` **[Stage]** The 'gold nuggets' that Google's feature extraction step pulls out of a page's HTML are structured data (such as JSON-LD), images and videos.
- [`D3-C324`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) (Day 3, How Search results are born) extends [`D2-C521`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) (Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet.)
  - `D3-C324` **[Stage]** Rich results differ from other search features because Google builds them from extra data that site owners provide, usually structured data and usually in JSON-LD format.
  - `D2-C521` **[Stage]** Structured data makes pages eligible to appear as rich results, Google's structured data talk said in its recap.
- [`D3-C325`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) (Day 3, How Search results are born) extends [`D2-C726`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) (Day 2, How does the index look like?)
  - `D3-C325` **[Stage]** AI Mode and AI Overviews are not rich results but standard search features: they need no structured data to function and work with the normal text results from Google's index.
  - `D2-C726` **[Stage]** AI Overviews and AI Mode use the same index structures and token-based snippets as classic web results, a point Google called important but not obvious.
- [`D3-C337`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) (Day 3, How Search results are born) extends [`D2-C454`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) (Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet.)
  - `D3-C337` **[Stage]** Review structured data lets a site specify how its users rated something; the review snippet shows an average star rating and often the number of reviews of a product, service or piece of content.
  - `D2-C454` **[Stage]** Structured data turns the loosely structured web into structured information that powers visual search features such as review stars and recipe filters (for example by preparation time).
- [`D3-C341`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) (Day 3, How Search results are born) extends [`D2-C614`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) (Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation)
  - `D3-C341` **[Stage]** Some countries rely a lot on social proof such as reviews, Google's speaker said, recalling a point from Google's Day 2 internationalisation talk.
  - `D2-C614` **[Stage]** According to consumer data shown on a slide in the talk (source not captured), US consumers judge product quality more by user feedback and reviews, while European shoppers seem to look more at brand reputation.
- [`D3-C365`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) (Day 3, Shopping on Search: Beyond the blue links) extends [`D2-C509`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) (Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet.)
  - `D3-C365` **[Stage]** Google added six Merchant Center feed attributes for AI shopping experiences: question and answer, documents, related products, item group title and variant option for variants, and popularity rank.
  - `D2-C509` **[Stage]** More shopping structured data news was left for a Day 3 talk by a Google colleague, Alex.
- [`D3-C378`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) (Day 3, Shopping on Search: Beyond the blue links) extends [`D2-C489`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) (Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet.)
  - `D3-C378` **[Stage]** Google Shopping called rich data with light structure the AI sweet spot: a little structure that helps the AI system understand the data, not deep, highly nested, complex structures.
  - `D2-C489` **[Stage]** Describing every semantic detail of a page in markup is probably not worth the effort; focus on the structured data that Google or other consumers actually use.
- [`D3-C383`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) (Day 3, Shopping on Search: Beyond the blue links) extends [`D2-C505`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) (Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet.)
  - `D3-C383` **[Stage]** In product markup, an offer's shipping and return information can point through a JSON-LD identifier (@id) to shipping and return data defined elsewhere.
  - `D2-C505` **[Stage]** Google's shopping structured data launches of the previous year (2025) added support for merchant loyalty programs and shipping policies, letting merchants define a policy at organisation level and specify details at product level.
- [`D3-C385`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) (Day 3, Shopping on Search: Beyond the blue links) extends [`D1-C065`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D3-C385` **[Stage]** Google Shopping uses its own crawler, Storebot (Storebot-Google), instead of Googlebot because it needs fresh product information, prices, availability and shipping details and therefore crawls much more often.
  - `D1-C065` **[Slide]** The scheduler is shared infrastructure that decides what to fetch and when and sends URLs to the crawler. Each team decides the scheduling parameters for its own user agents.
- [`D3-C396`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) (Day 3, Shopping on Search: Beyond the blue links) extends [`D2-C506`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) (Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet.)
  - `D3-C396` **[Stage]** Google works to make sure that what merchants can express in its shopping feeds can also be expressed in schema.org, adding vocabulary where schema.org lacks it, for example for product details.
  - `D2-C506` **[Stage]** Google's structured data speaker said that in the months before the event Google added support for validity dates on sale prices in product structured data, so merchants no longer need to rush to remove a sale price when the sale ends for fear it shows wrongly in snippets.
- [`D3-C440`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) (Day 3, Inside Search Console: What’s New & How to Use It) extends [`D1-C449`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D3-C440` **[Stage]** Google called AI reporting in Search Console an evolving space and expects the generative AI report to get richer, with more information in the future.
  - `D1-C449` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said he expected more AI reporting to launch in Search Console, without a timeline or a promise, because many people at Google care about giving site owners the information to understand and adapt to what happens in Search.
- [`D3-C442`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) (Day 3, Inside Search Console: What’s New & How to Use It) extends [`D2-C960`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S14-lightning-session-f-media.md) (Day 2, Lightning session F: Media)
  - `D3-C442` **[Stage]** Search Console launched platform properties, which bring social platforms into Search Console, about three or four months before the October 2026 event.
  - `D2-C960` **[Stage]** A community speaker said publishers can also verify their social accounts in Search Console, which makes it easier to track the performance of content repurposed for social platforms.
- [`D3-C468`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) (annotates Day 3, Inside Search Console: What’s New & How to Use It) extends [`D1-C025`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) (Day 1, What's new in the world of Search)
  - `D3-C468` **[Docs]** Google's social and video performance guide says that if you already claimed your Search profile, all of its verified accounts are added automatically as platform properties in Search Console.
  - `D1-C025` **[Slide]** Publishers and creators can claim a dedicated Search profile with a name, profile photo, cover image, bio, connected social and website accounts, pinned posts and links, and users can follow it.
- [`D3-C468`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) (annotates Day 3, Inside Search Console: What’s New & How to Use It) extends [`D2-C960`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S14-lightning-session-f-media.md) (Day 2, Lightning session F: Media)
  - `D3-C468` **[Docs]** Google's social and video performance guide says that if you already claimed your Search profile, all of its verified accounts are added automatically as platform properties in Search Console.
  - `D2-C960` **[Stage]** A community speaker said publishers can also verify their social accounts in Search Console, which makes it easier to track the performance of content repurposed for social platforms.
- [`D3-C469`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D1-C255`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI)
  - `D3-C469` **[Stage]** In a community lightning talk, agency founder Nik Vujic presented how his agency feeds Search Console and GA4 data to an LLM agent to support decisions for its clients.
  - `D1-C255` **[Stage]** A community speaker who is not a developer automated monthly SEO reports with Python in Visual Studio Code, using Claude and ChatGPT as coding partners and Google Cloud for access to the Search Console API.
- [`D3-C473`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (annotates Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D3-C417`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) (Day 3, Inside Search Console: What’s New & How to Use It)

  - `D3-C417` **[Stage]** Google said query groups are not built by matching query text alone: deciding which queries belong in which group goes beyond simple text filtering.
- [`D3-C477`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D1-C256`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI)
  - `D3-C477` **[Slide]** The community workflow's third step feeds the exported Search Console dataset into the agency's LLM agent, which queries the dataset and returns the evidence rather than a sample.
  - `D1-C256` **[Stage]** An agency's automated monthly SEO report follows four simple steps: the data comes in, a script processes it, AI summarises it and the result goes onto a dashboard.
- [`D3-C478`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D1-C256`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI)
  - `D3-C478` **[Slide]** Nik Vujic's slide said no agent is needed to start: pull the Search Console data, import it into any LLM and query it in conversation; his agency built its agent to have everything in one place.
  - `D1-C256` **[Stage]** An agency's automated monthly SEO report follows four simple steps: the data comes in, a script processes it, AI summarises it and the result goes onto a dashboard.
- [`D3-C487`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (annotates Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D2-C656`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) (Day 2, Calculating (some) signals)
  - `D3-C487` **[Analysis]** Google's ranking systems guide describes 'query deserves freshness' systems that show fresher content where it would be expected, which is narrower than a general preference for fresh content; refresh pages whose queries expect current information, and judge other refreshes by quality.
  - `D2-C656` **[Stage]** Freshness is a signal for queries that deserve fresh results ('query deserves freshness'): when a breaking event hits a city, such as possible closure of Barcelona's airport, users want really fresh results, not results from two weeks ago.
- [`D3-C492`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D3-C438`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) (Day 3, Inside Search Console: What’s New & How to Use It)

  - `D3-C438` **[Stage]** The regular Search Console Performance report still shows all traffic including AI features, while the generative AI view shows only impressions from AI surfaces.
- [`D3-C495`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D1-C124`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (annotates Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
