  - `D1-C124` **[Docs]** Google's launch post for the Generative AI performance reports in Search Console (3 June 2026; rolled out to all sites worldwide by 31 August 2026) lists impressions, pages, countries, devices (Search only) and dates, and no click or query metrics.
- [`D3-C495`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D3-C440`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) (Day 3, Inside Search Console: What’s New & How to Use It)
  - `D3-C495` **[Stage]** Nik Vujic said he hopes Search Console's generative AI report will get query data.
  - `D3-C440` **[Stage]** Google called AI reporting in Search Console an evolving space and expects the generative AI report to get richer, with more information in the future.
- [`D3-C497`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (annotates Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D1-C058`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D3-C497` **[Analysis]** Pages that do better in AI answers than in classic results do not refute Google's line that optimising for people is optimising for generative AI Search, since the comparison mixed Google's AI features with third-party LLMs; measure each surface separately, per page, before deciding what to change.
  - `D1-C058` **[Slide]** Optimising for people is optimising for generative AI Search.
- [`D3-C498`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (annotates Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D3-C438`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) (Day 3, Inside Search Console: What’s New & How to Use It)
  - `D3-C498` **[Docs]** Google's AI features guide says traffic from sites appearing in AI features such as AI Overviews and AI Mode is included in the overall search traffic in Search Console and reported in the Performance report within the Web search type.
  - `D3-C438` **[Stage]** The regular Search Console Performance report still shows all traffic including AI features, while the generative AI view shows only impressions from AI surfaces.
- [`D3-C501`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (annotates Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D3-C435`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) (annotates Day 3, Inside Search Console: What’s New & How to Use It)
  - `D3-C501` **[Analysis]** Before feeding a branded versus non-branded split to an LLM, spot-check a sample of queries in each group, since Google's AI-assisted classification can misidentify queries; on URL-path or subdomain properties, where the filter is unavailable, a regex query filter is the fallback.
  - `D3-C435` **[Analysis]** Review the filters and regexes that Search Console's AI-powered configuration proposes before trusting the numbers: Google's launch post calls the feature experimental, warns that AI can misinterpret requests, and limits it to the Search results Performance report (not Discover or News) and to configuration, not sorting or exporting.
- [`D3-C518`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D1-C057`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D3-C518` **[Stage]** A community speaker concluded that rankings and clicks no longer equal real business outcomes.
  - `D1-C057` **[Slide]** Myth: the old metrics don't work in the AI era. Google's answer: measure success through metrics that matter to your business.
- [`D3-C535`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (annotates Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D1-C062`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (annotates Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D3-C535` **[Docs]** Beyond Search Console, Google's AI features guide suggests tracking conversions and time spent on the site in tools such as Google Analytics to understand the value of traffic from AI features.
  - `D1-C062` **[Docs]** Google's guide for generative AI features recommends the Generative AI performance report in Search Console for measuring how content performs in generative AI features on Google Search and Discover.
- [`D3-C536`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (annotates Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D1-C057`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D3-C536` **[Docs]** A May 2025 Search Central blog post advised site owners to look at the overall value of visits from Search rather than focusing too much on clicks, using indicators of conversion such as sales, sign-ups, a more engaged audience or information lookups about the business.
  - `D1-C057` **[Slide]** Myth: the old metrics don't work in the AI era. Google's answer: measure success through metrics that matter to your business.
- [`D3-C542`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (annotates Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D1-C057`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D3-C542` **[Analysis]** Google's own line on Day 1 was to measure success by metrics that matter to the business, and its Generative AI performance report shows impressions but no clicks; together with the community talk this argues for a report that puts organic next to direct, branded paid search, conversions and revenue.
  - `D1-C057` **[Slide]** Myth: the old metrics don't work in the AI era. Google's answer: measure success through metrics that matter to your business.
- [`D3-C542`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) (annotates Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users) extends [`D1-C124`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (annotates Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D3-C542` **[Analysis]** Google's own line on Day 1 was to measure success by metrics that matter to the business, and its Generative AI performance report shows impressions but no clicks; together with the community talk this argues for a report that puts organic next to direct, branded paid search, conversions and revenue.
  - `D1-C124` **[Docs]** Google's launch post for the Generative AI performance reports in Search Console (3 June 2026; rolled out to all sites worldwide by 31 August 2026) lists impressions, pages, countries, devices (Search only) and dates, and no click or query metrics.
- [`D3-C562`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S16-mastering-the-messy-middle.md) (Day 3, Mastering the messy middle) extends [`D1-C018`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) (Day 1, What's new in the world of Search)
  - `D3-C562` **[Stage]** Google's research also counted easy access as part of AI's ease benefit: multimodal input, such as taking pictures, and low friction lower the barrier to entry.
  - `D1-C018` **[Slide]** One in six AI Mode searches is multimodal, using voice or images.
- [`D3-C569`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S16-mastering-the-messy-middle.md) (Day 3, Mastering the messy middle) extends [`D1-C004`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) (Day 1, Welcome and opening keynotes)
  - `D3-C569` **[Stage]** Google's research found that people who use AI run more searches than people who do not.
  - `D1-C004` **[Slide]** Google says users like AI Overviews and search more because of them, with early feedback overwhelmingly positive and satisfaction highest among 18–24 year olds.
- [`D3-C571`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S16-mastering-the-messy-middle.md) (Day 3, Mastering the messy middle) extends [`D1-C005`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) (Day 1, Welcome and opening keynotes)
  - `D3-C571` **[Stage]** Google's research found that people who use AI also visit more brand websites, because it is simply easier.
  - `D1-C005` **[Slide]** Google says AI Overviews help with new types of questions and lead users to visit a greater diversity of sites, with more total sites shown on the results page.
- [`D3-C602`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C201`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D3-C602` **[Stage]** Google said it knows hundreds of trillions of URLs (as of October 2026).
  - `D1-C201` **[Stage]** Google said there are trillions of URLs on the internet, or even more, that even Google cannot tell how many exist, and that some may never be discovered.
- [`D3-C606`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C466`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D3-C606` **[Stage]** For news sites in particular, Google said the refresh of a known URL can literally take seconds (the reading 'news sites' is likely but not certain).
  - `D1-C466` **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said news sites rarely need to worry about crawl budget, because Google crawls them aggressively given their constant flow of new content and new URLs.
- [`D3-C610`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C337`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D3-C610` **[Slide]** Google estimated that processing a sitemap takes about 24 hours on average, with a minimum of minutes.
  - `D1-C337` **[Stage]** An XML sitemap, a format from around 2005, gives Google, other search engines and potentially AI systems a list of the URLs a site wants crawled; Google called it nothing fancy but said it still uses sitemaps.
- [`D3-C611`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C337`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D3-C611` **[Slide]** If a sitemap is useful to Google and the site is of high quality, Google tries to refetch the sitemap within 14 days at most.
  - `D1-C337` **[Stage]** An XML sitemap, a format from around 2005, gives Google, other search engines and potentially AI systems a list of the URLs a site wants crawled; Google called it nothing fancy but said it still uses sitemaps.
- [`D3-C612`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C331`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) (Day 1, How crawling works)
  - `D3-C612` **[Slide]** Google may never fetch a lower-quality site's sitemap again: once it figures out the site is of lower quality, it no longer wants to fetch the sitemap.
  - `D1-C331` **[Stage]** Google's crawl scheduler very likely deprioritises a URL when the URL or its site is known to be historically spammy.
- [`D3-C613`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C085`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D3-C613` **[Slide]** Google estimated that a robots.txt update is picked up in about 24 hours, with a minimum of seconds and an end point of 25 hours on the slide.
  - `D1-C085` **[Docs]** Google generally caches robots.txt for up to 24 hours and reads only the first 500 KiB of the file.
- [`D3-C614`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C085`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D3-C614` **[Stage]** Google said its service level objective is to refresh robots.txt every 24 hours, as RFC 9309 calls for, though delays happen now and then.
  - `D1-C085` **[Docs]** Google generally caches robots.txt for up to 24 hours and reads only the first 500 KiB of the file.
- [`D3-C615`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C140`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D3-C615` **[Stage]** A site owner can submit robots.txt in Search Console to force Google to refresh it sooner.
  - `D1-C140` **[Docs]** Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt files Google found for the top 20 hosts of a Domain property, with their fetch status, warnings and errors; to test whether a specific URL is blocked, Google's help page points to the URL Inspection tool and to Google's open-source robots.txt library.
- [`D3-C617`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C493`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D3-C617` **[Slide]** Google's crawl chart puts a crawl capacity update at seconds when backing off, typically 4 hours or 1-2 weeks, and 1-3 weeks in recovery.
  - `D1-C493` **[Stage]** There is no easy way to tell whether a drop in Google's crawling comes from lower crawl demand or a lower crawl capacity limit; most of the time a capacity-limit drop is an abrupt step down.
- [`D3-C618`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C126`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (annotates Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D3-C618` **[Stage]** When a site starts serving 500 errors, Google lowers the crawl capacity allocated to the site within about four hours on average.
  - `D1-C126` **[Docs]** Google treats network timeouts, connection resets and DNS errors like 5xx server errors: crawling slows down immediately, and already indexed URLs that stay unreachable are removed from Google's index within days.
- [`D3-C618`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C354`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) (Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search)
  - `D3-C618` **[Stage]** When a site starts serving 500 errors, Google lowers the crawl capacity allocated to the site within about four hours on average.
  - `D1-C354` **[Stage]** Google slows crawling when a site returns 5xx errors, because a 5xx usually means the server, and often the whole site, cannot serve requests, and Google does not want to break the site.
- [`D3-C618`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C440`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D3-C618` **[Stage]** When a site starts serving 500 errors, Google lowers the crawl capacity allocated to the site within about four hours on average.
  - `D1-C440` **[Stage]** If a site's server cannot cope with the extra crawling that higher crawl demand brings, Google reduces its crawling of that site again.
- [`D3-C623`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C093`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D3-C623` **[Stage]** When Google notices the web getting excited about a few URLs on a site, it allocates more crawl demand to the whole site so it does not miss content useful to future searchers.
  - `D1-C093` **[Slide]** Crawl demand is driven by the quality of the site, the change frequency of its URLs and their popularity on the internet.
- [`D3-C623`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C377`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D3-C623` **[Stage]** When Google notices the web getting excited about a few URLs on a site, it allocates more crawl demand to the whole site so it does not miss content useful to future searchers.
  - `D1-C377` **[Stage]** The quality that drives crawl demand is the quality of the site as a whole, not the quality of an individual page.
- [`D3-C623`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C439`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D3-C623` **[Stage]** When Google notices the web getting excited about a few URLs on a site, it allocates more crawl demand to the whole site so it does not miss content useful to future searchers.
  - `D1-C439` **[Stage]** Very large, constantly changing sites get no special handling: when URLs change frequently or are useful to users, Google raises crawl demand and tries to raise its crawl capacity for the site, the same logic it applies to small sites.
- [`D3-C624`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C375`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D3-C624` **[Stage]** Crawl demand can also come from other Google products, such as Shopping, and the roughly 20-hour estimate covers only demand from Search.
  - `D1-C375` **[Stage]** Googlebot as a single standalone crawler is a historical idea: Google crawls through a centralised crawling infrastructure, so a request from a Google user agent in server logs is a request routed through that shared platform.
- [`D3-C626`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D2-C170`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript)
  - `D3-C626` **[Stage]** Google renders pages in two ways: immediately after crawling, or later through a queue-based process that runs elsewhere.
  - `D2-C170` **[Slide]** After processing, an indexable page is placed in Google's render queue to wait for rendering.
- [`D3-C627`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D2-C172`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript)
  - `D3-C627` **[Stage]** Content that JavaScript adds to a page is typically seen by Google's indexing system within a few hours, and at worst within weeks.
  - `D2-C172` **[Docs]** Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says a page may wait in the render queue for a few seconds but that it can take longer, and it gives no upper limit.
- [`D3-C628`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D2-C256`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) (Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript)
  - `D3-C628` **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said Google keeps saying it renders every URL on the internet and that he would say this is not true, though it is what he was told; he went on to say that Google's logs show the rendering queue cleared within weeks.
  - `D2-C256` **[Stage]** Google renders nearly all of the web by replicating what a browser does, using a real browser's rendering engine.
- [`D3-C642`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D2-C351`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication)
  - `D3-C642` **[Stage]** Google treats a site move as a complex canonicalization process in which every signal of the old site is recalculated and moved to the new one, and every indexing process has to run.
  - `D2-C351` **[Stage]** Google treats a site migration as deduplication across sites, in which the site owner says the old and the new domain are the same and that Google should pick the new domain, so deduplication also helps Google handle migrations.
- [`D3-C647`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D2-C500`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) (Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet.)
  - `D3-C647` **[Stage]** Google may never use structured data from a site it does not trust: once it sees markup it does not trust, it does not touch it.
  - `D2-C500` **[Stage]** Structured data that is not relevant to the page's content can be treated as abusive: Google's filters make it ineffective, and egregious cases can lead to a manual action.
- [`D3-C662`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D3-C294`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) (Day 3, What are quality updates)
  - `D3-C662` **[Slide]** Recovery after a core update typically takes 3 to 6 months once the site has put in work to regain traffic, and up to 6 months to a year, until the next core update.
  - `D3-C294` **[Stage]** After a core update a site can win back some of its rankings by improving the site as a whole.
- [`D3-C663`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D3-C286`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) (Day 3, What are quality updates)
  - `D3-C663` **[Slide]** Google estimated that a spam update affects sites within 1-2 days of the rollout, 1-2 weeks for continuous processing (said on stage as 2 weeks on average) and months for batch refreshes.
  - `D3-C286` **[Stage]** When spammers find loopholes that Google's systems miss, Google releases spam updates that change its systems to catch them.
- [`D3-C667`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (annotates Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D1-C528`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) (Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt)
  - `D3-C667` **[Docs]** Google's robots.txt guide says its crawlers update their cached copy of a site's robots.txt every 24 hours, and that the Request a recrawl option in Search Console's robots.txt report refreshes it faster.
  - `D1-C528` **[Stage]** Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt file as Google last fetched it, with a version history and the errors and successes of each fetch.
- [`D3-C676`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) (annotates Day 3, How long does it take to..?) extends [`D2-C131`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) (annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript)
  - `D3-C676` **[Analysis]** The stage doubt that every URL gets rendered sits beside Google's JavaScript guide, which says every page with a 200 status is queued for rendering unless a robots rule blocks indexing: queued is not the same as rendered, so do not rely on rendering for critical content.
  - `D2-C131` **[Docs]** Google's JavaScript SEO guide says Googlebot sends every page with a 200 HTTP status code to the rendering queue, whether or not it contains JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header tells Google not to index it, and Google uses the rendered HTML to index the page.
- [`D3-C680`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) (Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.) extends [`D1-C041`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D3-C680` **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said machine learning is about 50 years old and that Google has been using it for 'probably 30 years', starting with statistical models that made the 'Did you mean' feature possible.
  - `D1-C041` **[Slide]** Statistical models have been used at Google for over 20 years, for catching spam and originally for the 'Did you mean' feature.
- [`D3-C684`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) (Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.) extends [`D1-C042`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D3-C684` **[Stage]** Predictive language models have been used a lot in Search, and BERT is one: technically, in the purest sense, an LLM.
  - `D1-C042` **[Slide]** BERT is used in indexing to understand each word in the context of the whole sentence rather than one word at a time.
- [`D3-C686`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) (Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.) extends [`D2-C462`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) (annotates Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet.)
  - `D3-C686` **[Stage]** Hallucinations can happen with any AI model, and with current training methods there is no way to get rid of them.
  - `D2-C462` **[Docs]** Google's guidance on generative AI content warns that AI output can contain hallucinations and says AI-generated metadata, including structured data and image alt text, should be fact-checked before publishing and the markup validated.
- [`D3-C688`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) (Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.) extends [`D2-C939`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) (Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos)
  - `D3-C688` **[Stage]** Generative models, including image diffusion models, make things up when they lack information or because of issues in their training.
  - `D2-C939` **[Stage]** The diffusion models that generate images were built to generate images, not text, so they are typically poor at rendering text inside an image.
- [`D3-C690`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) (Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.) extends [`D3-C160`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) (Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality)
  - `D3-C690` **[Stage]** Quality raters cannot give a site a penalty or a manual action; their ratings are converted into labels that Google uses to improve its algorithms.
  - `D3-C160` **[Slide]** Google's slide said search quality raters cannot affect the rankings of individual sites.
- [`D3-C694`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) (Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.) extends [`D3-C284`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) (Day 3, What are quality updates)
  - `D3-C694` **[Stage]** Scaled content abuse is becoming a problem again: in the early 2000s pages were churned out with Perl or PHP scripts, and now the same is done with LLMs.
  - `D3-C284` **[Stage]** Reviewing the spam slide, the speaker said link spam would probably be replaced with scaled content abuse as the spam type worth talking about today.
- [`D3-C695`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) (Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.) extends [`D2-C611`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) (annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation)
  - `D3-C695` **[Stage]** The cheaper tokens become, the more AI slop is created, and Google counts AI slop as scaled content abuse.
  - `D2-C611` **[Docs]** Google's spam policies define scaled content abuse as generating many pages mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value to users, no matter how they are created, and list automated translating of scraped content among the examples.
- [`D3-C697`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) (Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.) extends [`D2-C611`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) (annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation)
  - `D3-C697` **[Stage]** Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines point out that the tool used to create content is not the problem, but how it was used and what for.
  - `D2-C611` **[Docs]** Google's spam policies define scaled content abuse as generating many pages mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value to users, no matter how they are created, and list automated translating of scraped content among the examples.
- [`D3-C700`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) (Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.) extends [`D2-C941`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) (Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos)
  - `D3-C700` **[Slide]** Google's closing slide said to use AI responsibly because AI hallucinates, and, especially when creating content briefs with AI, to make sure not to add to the sea of AI slop already flooding the internet.
  - `D2-C941` **[Stage]** Sites that use AI-generated images or videos should make sure they work for users, check them for hallucinations and regenerate them where needed.
- [`D3-C701`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) (Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.) extends [`D1-C038`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D3-C701` **[Slide]** Google's closing slide said AI on Google is just SEO: AI features on Google Search use exactly the same processes as traditional results, so no new acronym is needed, as none was for mobile-first indexing or structured data.
  - `D1-C038` **[Slide]** AI Mode and AI Overviews use the same crawling and the same index as Search. At serving they add grounding on the Search index and query fan-out.
- [`D3-C708`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) (Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.) extends [`D1-C227`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI)
  - `D3-C708` **[Stage]** Google does not tell lightning-talk and poster speakers what to talk about; they bring their own ideas.
  - `D1-C227` **[Stage]** Google received close to 200 submissions for the community lightning talks of the Deep Dive, reviewed them over about a month, and gave each selected community speaker seven minutes on stage.

## Contradicts (5)

- [`D1-C296`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI) contradicts [`D1-C049`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) (Day 1, What's new in the world of Search)
  - `D1-C296` **[Stage]** A community speaker argued for adopting the GEO label as the industry's chance to leave behind the bad reputation SEO built, unlike Google's view earlier the same day that the new name is not needed.
  - `D1-C049` **[Stage]** Gary Illyes argued that GEO is a label invented to create a new field and is not needed. Understanding how SEO works is enough.
- [`D1-C296`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) (Day 1, Lightning session A: Automation and AI) contradicts [`D1-C050`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D1-C296` **[Stage]** A community speaker argued for adopting the GEO label as the industry's chance to leave behind the bad reputation SEO built, unlike Google's view earlier the same day that the new name is not needed.
  - `D1-C050` **[Slide]** Google's answer to 'SEO is dead, long live GEO' is not to worry about the name: good SEO is good GEO and AEO.
- [`D2-C325`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) (Day 2, Understanding what's on a page) contradicts [`D1-C039`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D2-C325` **[Stage]** Tokenization for AI models such as Gemini, in training and in inference, differs from tokenization for Search, although Gary Illyes qualified this with 'or mostly'.
  - `D1-C039` **[Slide]** Gemini is not part of Search, but it uses crawlers for data, shares some technologies such as tokenization and deduping, and grounds on the Search index.
- [`D2-C393`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication) contradicts [`D1-C115`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) (annotates Day 1, session not recorded)
  - `D2-C393` **[Stage]** Google's speaker said that pointing rel=canonical from the pages of a paginated set to the first page can sometimes make sense depending on the goal, for example to make a category page more visible, but that it affects canonicalization and deduplication.
  - `D1-C115` **[Docs]** Google's crawlers do not click buttons. Each page in a series needs its own URL and an `<a href>` link to the next page, should not use page 1 as its canonical, and rel=next and rel=prev are no longer used.
- [`D2-C429`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) (Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves) contradicts [`D2-C348`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) (Day 2, Handling web duplication)
  - `D2-C429` **[Stage]** A community speaker said pages carry different link equity, and a canonical leader that is not the strongest page in its group is technically valid but most likely suboptimal for ranking, so the strongest page should be the leader.
  - `D2-C348` **[Slide]** Google forwards the signals attached to every URL in a duplicate cluster, such as links, to the representative URL, so that nothing is lost by showing only one URL.

## Updates (1)

- [`D1-C125`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) (annotates Day 1, What's new in the world of Search) updates [`D1-C026`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) (annotates Day 1, What's new in the world of Search)
  - `D1-C125` **[Docs]** Since 16 September 2026, US publishers and creators qualify for a Search profile with 10,000 followers across YouTube, Instagram, X or TikTok, and media organisations can claim and manage profiles for all their sub-brands from one login.
  - `D1-C026` **[Docs]** Search profiles launched on 4 June 2026, in the US first, for creators and publishers with a sizable following on at least one major social or video platform. They appear in knowledge panels and Discover.

## Answers (70)

- [`D1-C047`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?) answers [`D1-C046`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D1-C047` **[Slide]** Google's answer was that ML-based ranking systems are trained on content written by humans for humans, so they understand and promote natural content better.
  - `D1-C046` **[Slide]** A Google slide headed 'Your Question' raised whether Google can distinguish between AI-written and human-written content, presented on stage as the question this topic usually prompts rather than one asked live.
- [`D1-C210`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?) answers [`D1-C046`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) (Day 1, How Search works and where's AI?)
  - `D1-C210` **[Stage]** Google said it is not really trying to tell AI-written from human-written content, because it cares more about the quality of content than about how it was created.
  - `D1-C046` **[Slide]** A Google slide headed 'Your Question' raised whether Google can distinguish between AI-written and human-written content, presented on stage as the question this topic usually prompts rather than one asked live.
- [`D1-C381`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) answers [`D1-C380`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C381` **[Stage]** Not every site needs to worry about crawl budget, and this has always been so: a site with fewer than a few thousand URLs likely has no crawl budget problem, and a larger site does not necessarily have one either.
  - `D1-C380` **[Stage]** An audience member asked, in a question submitted before the event, whether crawl budget is still an SEO priority in 2026 or only relevant for very large sites.
- [`D1-C388`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) answers [`D1-C387`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C388` **[Stage]** AI Mode is a feature that sits on top of Google's existing crawling infrastructure, so Google does not crawl a site more because of AI Mode.
  - `D1-C387` **[Stage]** An audience member asked, in questions submitted before the event, how often Googlebot should be expected to visit a site now that AI Mode has rolled out, and whether AI means more crawling.
- [`D1-C389`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) answers [`D1-C387`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C389` **[Stage]** Google expects sites to see more crawling overall, because many other services, including AI services, now crawl the web besides Google.
  - `D1-C387` **[Stage]** An audience member asked, in questions submitted before the event, how often Googlebot should be expected to visit a site now that AI Mode has rolled out, and whether AI means more crawling.
- [`D1-C391`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) answers [`D1-C390`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C391` **[Stage]** A higher crawl rate does not make a URL rank better; it only means Google checks the site more often.
  - `D1-C390` **[Stage]** An audience member asked, in a question submitted before the event, whether crawl frequency affects the ranking position of a URL.
- [`D1-C392`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget) answers [`D1-C390`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) (Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget)
  - `D1-C392` **[Stage]** Frequent crawling is usually a consequence, not a cause: Google visiting a site more often tends to signal that people are interested in the site and that its content is of high quality.
  - `D1-C390` **[Stage]** An audience member asked, in a question submitted before the event, whether crawl frequency affects the ranking position of a URL.
- [`D1-C423`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C422`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C423` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said many AI crawlers are less sophisticated than search crawlers: in server logs, search crawlers tend to follow where a site changes and which pages are valuable, while AI crawlers may simply work through a site in order, which he put down to less crawling experience and different priorities.
  - `D1-C422` **[Stage]** An audience member asked, in a question submitted at registration, what the biggest difference is between crawling for search and crawling for AI models.
- [`D1-C424`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C422`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C424` **[Stage]** Google's search crawling works to keep content fresh and to understand which pages change frequently, whereas many AI systems crawl a site with no understanding of it and take everything.
  - `D1-C422` **[Stage]** An audience member asked, in a question submitted at registration, what the biggest difference is between crawling for search and crawling for AI models.
- [`D1-C425`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C422`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C425` **[Stage]** Crawling for AI model training differs from search crawling because training mainly needs a very large number of tokens, and it matters little which pages they come from.
  - `D1-C422` **[Stage]** An audience member asked, in a question submitted at registration, what the biggest difference is between crawling for search and crawling for AI models.
- [`D1-C428`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C427`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C428` **[Stage]** Mainstream crawlers from Google, other large search engines and AI companies try to follow robots.txt, so implementing robots.txt correctly is the way to stop them doing something specific on a site.
  - `D1-C427` **[Stage]** An audience question asked how to make sure bots behave well beyond robots.txt.
- [`D1-C429`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C427`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C429` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said crawlers that ignore robots.txt and cause a nuisance are better treated as a scraping problem than as a crawling problem.
  - `D1-C427` **[Stage]** An audience question asked how to make sure bots behave well beyond robots.txt.
- [`D1-C439`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C438`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C439` **[Stage]** Very large, constantly changing sites get no special handling: when URLs change frequently or are useful to users, Google raises crawl demand and tries to raise its crawl capacity for the site, the same logic it applies to small sites.
  - `D1-C438` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how Google prioritises crawling and indexing for very large real-time sites, such as sports sites, whose content changes constantly and is largely near-duplicate across seasons.
- [`D1-C440`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C438`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C440` **[Stage]** If a site's server cannot cope with the extra crawling that higher crawl demand brings, Google reduces its crawling of that site again.
  - `D1-C438` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how Google prioritises crawling and indexing for very large real-time sites, such as sports sites, whose content changes constantly and is largely near-duplicate across seasons.
- [`D1-C442`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C441`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C442` **[Stage]** Log files alone cannot show crawl inefficiency because they do not reveal where Google's crawl limit for the site lies; many similar URLs being crawled may not matter if the site is nowhere near that limit.
  - `D1-C441` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how to tell, from log files or by other methods, whether Google is spending crawl budget inefficiently on a site.
- [`D1-C443`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C441`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C443` **[Stage]** To judge crawl efficiency, check Search Console's Crawl Stats report: whether total crawling has plateaued over time, and whether the average response time shows the server is fast enough or is limiting Googlebot.
  - `D1-C441` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how to tell, from log files or by other methods, whether Google is spending crawl budget inefficiently on a site.
- [`D1-C444`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C441`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C444` **[Stage]** Log files are worth checking on sites with filter parameters or complicated URLs, because crawlers can easily wander off into URLs that make no sense for the site.
  - `D1-C441` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how to tell, from log files or by other methods, whether Google is spending crawl budget inefficiently on a site.
- [`D1-C445`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C441`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C445` **[Stage]** One fix for parameter variants of a URL is to work out the normalised URL and redirect the variants to it: the redirects cost crawl budget at first, but leave the site with a clean slate.
  - `D1-C441` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how to tell, from log files or by other methods, whether Google is spending crawl budget inefficiently on a site.
- [`D1-C449`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C448`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C449` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said he expected more AI reporting to launch in Search Console, without a timeline or a promise, because many people at Google care about giving site owners the information to understand and adapt to what happens in Search.
  - `D1-C448` **[Stage]** An audience member asked what changes to expect in Search Console's reporting on Google's AI features.
- [`D1-C450`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C448`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C450` **[Stage]** Google said reporting on AI features should not simply mirror classic search results, because users get more information before they click and interact with pages differently, so it first has to work out which data would be useful and actionable.
  - `D1-C448` **[Stage]** An audience member asked what changes to expect in Search Console's reporting on Google's AI features.
- [`D1-C452`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C451`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C452` **[Stage]** Query data for AI features is hard to provide because people ask AI very different kinds of questions that do not map back to keywords as in classic search, and the data would have to be grouped to protect privacy while staying useful.
  - `D1-C451` **[Stage]** An audience member asked for data on AI features as a feedback channel for improving content, as an alternative to prompt-tracking tools.
- [`D1-C454`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C453`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C454` **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said llms.txt does not matter for Google Search right now and that he does not expect it to, while adding that he had been wrong before.
  - `D1-C453` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether llms.txt matters, given that Google had said it does not while PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse advocate it and audit tools ask site owners to create the file.
- [`D1-C455`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C453`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C455` **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said llms.txt matters to some people, which is why tools such as Lighthouse add checks for it, so both sides of the debate are right in their own context.
  - `D1-C453` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether llms.txt matters, given that Google had said it does not while PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse advocate it and audit tools ask site owners to create the file.
- [`D1-C456`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C453`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C456` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said he knew of no plan for Google to use llms.txt, though it could happen, and that a possible future change is no reason to implement it now.
  - `D1-C453` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether llms.txt matters, given that Google had said it does not while PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse advocate it and audit tools ask site owners to create the file.
- [`D1-C457`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C453`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C457` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said most llms.txt files he had seen are generated automatically by a setting in SEO plugins, so if Google Search ever made llms.txt matter, a site could add one by ticking a checkbox.
  - `D1-C453` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether llms.txt matters, given that Google had said it does not while PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse advocate it and audit tools ask site owners to create the file.
- [`D1-C458`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C453`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C458` **[Stage]** A Google panelist objected that llms.txt is designed for supposedly intelligent systems that should be able to parse a website.
  - `D1-C453` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether llms.txt matters, given that Google had said it does not while PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse advocate it and audit tools ask site owners to create the file.
- [`D1-C459`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C453`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C459` **[Stage]** A Google panelist compared llms.txt to the old meta keywords debate: an AI agent should not blindly trust what a site says about its own authority, just as a site calling itself the best car insurance site is no reason to stop looking at others.
  - `D1-C453` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether llms.txt matters, given that Google had said it does not while PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse advocate it and audit tools ask site owners to create the file.
- [`D1-C462`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C461`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C462` **[Stage]** Google said it knew of no plans to add crawl stats to the Search Console API, because that would be a completely new part of the API.
  - `D1-C461` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether and when crawl stats will be added to the Search Console API.
- [`D1-C463`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C461`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C463` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said adding a report that is a variation of the Performance report to the Search Console API would be easier than adding crawl stats, because the Performance report is already in the API.
  - `D1-C461` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether and when crawl stats will be added to the Search Console API.
- [`D1-C464`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C461`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C464` **[Stage]** Google's Search Relations team talks with the Search Console team about the API more than before, partly because with so many vibe-coded systems around it is very easy to just say 'use the Search Console API to do something', and it is annoying when Search Console has no API for that.
  - `D1-C461` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether and when crawl stats will be added to the Search Console API.
- [`D1-C466`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C465`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C466` **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said news sites rarely need to worry about crawl budget, because Google crawls them aggressively given their constant flow of new content and new URLs.
  - `D1-C465` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how a large news site can tell whether crawl budget is limiting how fast new articles are discovered (within minutes), and which statistics in Search Console and the logs show this.
- [`D1-C467`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C465`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C467` **[Stage]** To check that new content is crawled fast enough, Gary Illyes advised measuring the time between publishing a URL and Googlebot's first crawl of it: ideally it stays flat or falls, and only a rising trend calls for investigation.
  - `D1-C465` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how a large news site can tell whether crawl budget is limiting how fast new articles are discovered (within minutes), and which statistics in Search Console and the logs show this.
- [`D1-C468`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C465`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C468` **[Stage]** When new URLs are picked up more slowly, Gary Illyes advised checking the log files for URLs that Google crawls and recrawls a lot and judging whether they are useful.
  - `D1-C465` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how a large news site can tell whether crawl budget is limiting how fast new articles are discovered (within minutes), and which statistics in Search Console and the logs show this.
- [`D1-C469`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C465`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C469` **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said disallowing a section that should not be crawled, such as /ads, in a Googlebot group in robots.txt shifts crawl budget to the rest of the site.
  - `D1-C465` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how a large news site can tell whether crawl budget is limiting how fast new articles are discovered (within minutes), and which statistics in Search Console and the logs show this.
- [`D1-C472`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C471`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C472` **[Stage]** cats.txt was created by an SEO as a satirical take on llms.txt, to show that crawlers fetch whatever files they are given, so requests for llms.txt in server logs do not mean the file is important.
  - `D1-C471` **[Stage]** An audience question noted that a cats.txt file received more crawler requests than llms.txt in the server logs and asked how important that is.
- [`D1-C473`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C471`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C473` **[Stage]** Files such as cats.txt have no importance for Google Search: if a site links to one, Googlebot will find and crawl it, but it has no other effect.
  - `D1-C471` **[Stage]** An audience question noted that a cats.txt file received more crawler requests than llms.txt in the server logs and asked how important that is.
- [`D1-C475`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C474`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C475` **[Stage]** There is no sweet spot to find for a sitemap: technically it should list every URL you want indexed, so that Google can find each of them.
  - `D1-C474` **[Stage]** An audience member asked where the sweet spot is for a sitemap that misses nothing but does not overflow Search Console.
- [`D1-C477`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C476`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C477` **[Stage]** In a migration about four or five years before the event, Google consolidated 12 or 14 of its blogs in different languages, a Help Center and its old developers site into one site.
  - `D1-C476` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how to plan a site migration so that it does not leave large numbers of URLs not indexed.
- [`D1-C478`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C476`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C478` **[Stage]** The first priority in Google's own site consolidation was to identify the popular URLs people care about and make sure the migration did not damage them.
  - `D1-C476` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how to plan a site migration so that it does not leave large numbers of URLs not indexed.
- [`D1-C479`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C476`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C479` **[Stage]** Where content was duplicated across languages, Google's own site consolidation redirected two language versions into one, giving both old URLs one target path to redirect to.
  - `D1-C476` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how to plan a site migration so that it does not leave large numbers of URLs not indexed.
- [`D1-C482`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C481`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C482` **[Stage]** Nearly all mainstream AI crawlers and AI systems use their own user agents, so robots.txt can set a separate policy for each; at the event OpenAI was said to have three or four, Anthropic a few and Microsoft some.
  - `D1-C481` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether Google plans dedicated user agents for AI, as OpenAI has several, so that site owners can control AI access separately from Googlebot and analyse it in their logs.
- [`D1-C483`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C481`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C483` **[Stage]** A Google panelist doubted that setting different robots.txt policies per AI crawler makes practical sense yet, because nobody knows how these systems will develop.
  - `D1-C481` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether Google plans dedicated user agents for AI, as OpenAI has several, so that site owners can control AI access separately from Googlebot and analyse it in their logs.
- [`D1-C484`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C481`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C484` **[Stage]** A Google panelist called blocking all AI crawlers while allowing search crawlers such as Googlebot, Bingbot and Applebot a personal, philosophical decision that every site owner can make.
  - `D1-C481` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether Google plans dedicated user agents for AI, as OpenAI has several, so that site owners can control AI access separately from Googlebot and analyse it in their logs.
- [`D1-C485`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C481`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C485` **[Stage]** To opt out of Google's AI training, a site can use the Google-Extended token in robots.txt.
  - `D1-C481` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether Google plans dedicated user agents for AI, as OpenAI has several, so that site owners can control AI access separately from Googlebot and analyse it in their logs.
- [`D1-C487`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C481`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C487` **[Stage]** A Google panelist said Apple offers a robots.txt control for Applebot similar to Google-Extended, so a site can allow Applebot for search while opting out of Apple's AI use.
  - `D1-C481` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether Google plans dedicated user agents for AI, as OpenAI has several, so that site owners can control AI access separately from Googlebot and analyse it in their logs.
- [`D1-C488`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C481`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C488` **[Stage]** When logs show an unknown crawler fetching a lot, search for its user agent online to find the robots.txt token that controls it; the mainstream crawlers that send the most traffic can all be controlled this way.
  - `D1-C481` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether Google plans dedicated user agents for AI, as OpenAI has several, so that site owners can control AI access separately from Googlebot and analyse it in their logs.
- [`D1-C489`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C481`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C489` **[Stage]** A Google panelist called a default-deny robots.txt, which blocks every crawler and allows only chosen ones, a bad pattern because the site owner does not know what is being blocked.
  - `D1-C481` **[Stage]** An audience member asked whether Google plans dedicated user agents for AI, as OpenAI has several, so that site owners can control AI access separately from Googlebot and analyse it in their logs.
- [`D1-C491`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C490`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C491` **[Stage]** If paginated pages are replaced by a load-more button or infinite scroll without crawlable links to them, Google will not see the further pages at all.
  - `D1-C490` **[Stage]** An audience member asked what happens to thousands of crawled and indexed paginated category and tag pages if they are replaced by a single page with a JavaScript load-more button, and whether the old pages should then redirect to the canonical first page.
- [`D1-C493`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C545`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C493` **[Stage]** There is no easy way to tell whether a drop in Google's crawling comes from lower crawl demand or a lower crawl capacity limit; most of the time a capacity-limit drop is an abrupt step down.
  - `D1-C545` **[Stage]** An audience member asked, for very large sites of about 100 million pages, what signs show that a site is limited by crawl budget, and how to tell a crawl capacity limit problem from a crawl demand problem.
- [`D1-C494`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C545`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C494` **[Stage]** To check whether Google lowered a site's crawl capacity limit, look at the number of connections Googlebot opens to the site: if it has dropped, the capacity limit changed.
  - `D1-C545` **[Stage]** An audience member asked, for very large sites of about 100 million pages, what signs show that a site is limited by crawl budget, and how to tell a crawl capacity limit problem from a crawl demand problem.
- [`D1-C114`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C490`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C114` **[Stage]** A Google panelist called pagination one of the trickiest things in web development and said switching to infinite scroll or a load-more button is risky, depending on what you want to achieve, because Googlebot does not click buttons.
  - `D1-C490` **[Stage]** An audience member asked what happens to thousands of crawled and indexed paginated category and tag pages if they are replaced by a single page with a JavaScript load-more button, and whether the old pages should then redirect to the canonical first page.
- [`D1-C540`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C476`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C540` **[Stage]** Asked how to plan a migration that does not leave many URLs unindexed, a Google panelist said the answer is probably not sitemaps: decide what matters from the business's perspective (for example whether to consolidate languages); listing the new URLs in a sitemap is probably a good idea and cannot hurt, but it is not the main tool.
  - `D1-C476` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how to plan a site migration so that it does not leave large numbers of URLs not indexed.
- [`D1-C546`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A) answers [`D1-C545`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) (Day 1, Q&A)
  - `D1-C546` **[Stage]** A Google panelist illustrated a crawl capacity limit drop as a step down in the site's hostload, for example from 10 to 5, which the panelist said means Googlebot then makes up to five requests per second (the recording adds 'per connection', which is unclear).
  - `D1-C545` **[Stage]** An audience member asked, for very large sites of about 100 million pages, what signs show that a site is limited by crawl budget, and how to tell a crawl capacity limit problem from a crawl demand problem.
- [`D2-C002`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C001`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C002` **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that good HTML sitemaps are hard to make for large sites.
  - `D2-C001` **[Slide]** An audience member asked whether HTML sitemaps still matter for large sites, whether they improve Googlebot's crawl discovery and whether they pass link equity to deeper pages.
- [`D2-C820`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C001`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C820` **[Slide]** Google's Q&A slide advised large sites to rely on hub pages, such as category pages, that link out to their important pages, instead of on HTML sitemaps.
  - `D2-C001` **[Slide]** An audience member asked whether HTML sitemaps still matter for large sites, whether they improve Googlebot's crawl discovery and whether they pass link equity to deeper pages.
- [`D2-C003`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C001`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C003` **[Slide]** Google's Q&A slide on HTML sitemaps added that category hub pages linking to a site's important pages have the extra benefit that they may also be useful to users.
  - `D2-C001` **[Slide]** An audience member asked whether HTML sitemaps still matter for large sites, whether they improve Googlebot's crawl discovery and whether they pass link equity to deeper pages.
- [`D2-C010`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C009`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C010` **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that whether to keep a temporarily out-of-stock product page or redirect it depends on how important that product page is to users.
  - `D2-C009` **[Slide]** An audience member asked whether a product detail page that is out of stock for two to three months should keep returning 200 with links to similar products, or be 302-redirected to a similar product or to its parent product listing page.
- [`D2-C011`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C009`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C011` **[Slide]** Google's Q&A slide on out-of-stock product pages said users might wait months for some products, or even pre-order them if the site offers pre-ordering.
  - `D2-C009` **[Slide]** An audience member asked whether a product detail page that is out of stock for two to three months should keep returning 200 with links to similar products, or be 302-redirected to a similar product or to its parent product listing page.
- [`D2-C017`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C015`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C017` **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that a sitemap listed in the robots.txt file can be picked up by any crawler, not only by Google's.
  - `D2-C015` **[Slide]** An audience member asked whether the sitemap link should be included in robots.txt, noting that many websites include it but that it was missing from an earlier robots.txt slide by a Google speaker, which the question called 'Gary's slide'.
- [`D2-C018`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C015`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C018` **[Slide]** Google's Q&A slide said that a sitemap not listed in robots.txt has to be submitted instead, for example in Search Console.
  - `D2-C015` **[Slide]** An audience member asked whether the sitemap link should be included in robots.txt, noting that many websites include it but that it was missing from an earlier robots.txt slide by a Google speaker, which the question called 'Gary's slide'.
- [`D2-C020`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C019`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C020` **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as a noindex because some extremely important sites disallow their most important pages, by accident or out of ignorance.
  - `D2-C019` **[Slide]** An audience member noted that a robots.txt block does not mean noindex and that explaining this to developers is a constant struggle, and asked why Google does not treat a robots.txt block as a noindex.
- [`D2-C021`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C019`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C021` **[Slide]** Google's Q&A slide said Google does not index the content of pages disallowed in robots.txt, but users will still find the URLs of those pages in Search.
  - `D2-C019` **[Slide]** An audience member noted that a robots.txt block does not mean noindex and that explaining this to developers is a constant struggle, and asked why Google does not treat a robots.txt block as a noindex.
- [`D2-C838`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C001`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C838` **[Stage]** Answering whether HTML sitemaps still matter for large sites, Google said a site that wants one can make one, but that the effort is better spent on hub pages such as category pages.
  - `D2-C001` **[Slide]** An audience member asked whether HTML sitemaps still matter for large sites, whether they improve Googlebot's crawl discovery and whether they pass link equity to deeper pages.
- [`D2-C840`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C839`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C840` **[Stage]** Google answered that several sloppy migrations on one domain can cause many effects in the short term, and noted that migrations concern indexing as well as crawling, a subject a later Day 2 talk would cover.
  - `D2-C839` **[Stage]** An audience member asked how several sloppy migrations on the same domain can affect Googlebot's crawling.
- [`D2-C841`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C009`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C841` **[Stage]** Google contrasted out-of-stock products a buyer will wait for, such as a rare watch battery that matters to them, with easily replaced products, such as a particular cheese, for which the buyer simply picks a similar product instead of waiting.
  - `D2-C009` **[Slide]** An audience member asked whether a product detail page that is out of stock for two to three months should keep returning 200 with links to similar products, or be 302-redirected to a similar product or to its parent product listing page.
- [`D2-C842`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C015`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C842` **[Stage]** Google said listing the sitemap in robots.txt is fine, as many websites do.
  - `D2-C015` **[Slide]** An audience member asked whether the sitemap link should be included in robots.txt, noting that many websites include it but that it was missing from an earlier robots.txt slide by a Google speaker, which the question called 'Gary's slide'.
- [`D2-C843`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C015`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C843` **[Stage]** Google pointed out the trade-off of listing a sitemap in robots.txt: anyone can then see the sitemap, which a site may not want.
  - `D2-C015` **[Slide]** An audience member asked whether the sitemap link should be included in robots.txt, noting that many websites include it but that it was missing from an earlier robots.txt slide by a Google speaker, which the question called 'Gary's slide'.
- [`D2-C844`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C019`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C844` **[Stage]** Google illustrated why it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as noindex with an extremely important site, such as a national tax authority, that blocks very important PDF files with robots.txt: Google cannot index the PDFs' content but can at least show their URLs in search results.
  - `D2-C019` **[Slide]** An audience member noted that a robots.txt block does not mean noindex and that explaining this to developers is a constant struggle, and asked why Google does not treat a robots.txt block as a noindex.
- [`D2-C845`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C019`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C845` **[Stage]** Google said very few URLs disallowed by robots.txt are in its index, compared with the index as a whole (no figure given).
  - `D2-C019` **[Slide]** An audience member noted that a robots.txt block does not mean noindex and that explaining this to developers is a constant struggle, and asked why Google does not treat a robots.txt block as a noindex.
- [`D2-C846`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!) answers [`D2-C019`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) (Day 2, Welcome to indexing day!)
  - `D2-C846` **[Stage]** Google said a URL disallowed by robots.txt might still be indexed if the URL is important, in which case the URL is indexed but not its content.
  - `D2-C019` **[Slide]** An audience member noted that a robots.txt block does not mean noindex and that explaining this to developers is a constant struggle, and asked why Google does not treat a robots.txt block as a noindex.
